question: Y127
answer:
ANSWER

In the text of section 378 of the Companies Act 2006 (c. 46) stated to be up to date with all changes in force on or before 22 November 2026 — which encompasses the 20 November 2026 currency date — the small-donations exception states:

  Ceiling: £5,000.
  Measuring period: the period of 12 months ending with the date on which the donation in question is made (a rolling, backward-looking 12-month look-back), NOT the financial year and NOT the accounting reference period.

AUTHORITY AND VERIFICATION

- Provision: Companies Act 2006, Part 14 (Control of political donations and expenditure), Exemptions, section 378, marginal heading 'Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period'.
- Text (verbatim, from the fetched pages):

  '378 Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period U.K.

  (1) Authorisation under this Part is not needed for a donation except to the extent that the total amount of—
    (a) that donation, and
    (b) other relevant donations made in the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made,
  exceeds £5,000.

  (2) In this section—
    "donation" means a donation to a political party or other political organisation or to an independent election candidate; and
    "other relevant donations" means—
      (a) in relation to a donation made by a company that is not a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company or by any of its subsidiaries;
      (b) in relation to a donation made by a company that is a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company, by any holding company of that company or by any other subsidiary of any such holding company.

  (3) If or to the extent that a donation is exempt by virtue of this section from the requirement of authorisation under this Part, it shall be disregarded in determining what donations are authorised by any resolution passed for the purposes of this Part.'

- Version control (why this holds for 20 November 2026):
  * legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2024-01-04 — status banner: 'Section 378 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 22 November 2026'; text as quoted above.
  * legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2014-06-13 — same banner, identical wording.
  * legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/2026-04-06 — Part 14 point-in-time view as at 06/04/2026, same banner, identical s.378 wording.
  * legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/contents/2016-04-06 — table of contents lists '378. Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period'.
  * King's Printer PDF of the Act as enacted (ukpga_20060046_en_001.pdf) — s.378 as enacted is word-for-word the same.
  * The 'Alternative versions' control lists only 01/10/2007 (commencement amendment) and the point-in-time dates above; there is no amending instrument recorded against s.378. Commencement note I1: 'S. 378 wholly in force at 1.10.2008 ... in force for certain purposes at 1.10.2007 (E.W.S.), 1.11.2007 (N.I.) and otherwise in force at 1.10.2008 by S.I. 2007/2194'. The section has therefore been textually stable from commencement to the stated currency date, so the figure is the same whichever in-force version on or before 20 November 2026 is consulted.
  * Caveat to record: the banner adds 'There are changes that may be brought into force at a future date.' Those prospective changes are not in force and do not form part of the text current through 20 November 2026; no such change is shown as touching the £5,000 figure or the 12-month period.

SCOPE POINT THE COMPANY SECRETARY SHOULD NOT MISS

Section 378 is not a small-company audit-exemption provision. Audit exemption for small companies sits in Part 16 (ss.475–479 and Schedule 5A). Section 378 is the de minimis exemption from the Part 14 requirement of shareholder authorisation for political donations and political expenditure. The figure above is a political-donation ceiling; it has nothing to do with charity law, donation covenants, gift aid or accounting thresholds. If the secretary's question is really about audit exemption, the relevant thresholds (turnover / balance sheet total / employees) must be taken from Part 16 as amended, not from s.378.

HOW THE EXCEPTION OPERATES (procedure for applying it)

Step 1 — Characterise the payment. Is it a 'donation' within s.378(2), i.e. a donation to a political party, other political organisation, or an independent election candidate? The extended meaning of 'political donation' is in s.364 and 'political expenditure' in s.365; ss.374–377 exempt trade union subscriptions, trade association membership subscriptions, all-party parliamentary groups and expenditure exempted by order. Only a s.378 donation is tested against the £5,000 figure.

Step 2 — Fix the measuring window. Take the date the donation is made and look back exactly 12 months from that date. This is a rolling window, recalculated for every donation; it is not the company's financial year, not the accounting reference period under s.391, and not a calendar year.

Step 3 — Aggregate the right population. Add to the candidate donation every 'other relevant donation' made in that 12-month window:
  - company that is not a subsidiary: donations by that company and by any of its subsidiaries;
  - company that is a subsidiary: donations by that company, by any holding company of it, and by any other subsidiary of any such holding company.
  The test is group-wide and per donor group, not per donor entity.

Step 4 — Apply the ceiling. Authorisation under Part 14 is not needed except to the extent the aggregate exceeds £5,000. The £5,000 is a threshold, not a cap: the first £5,000 of aggregate in the window is exempt, and only the excess requires authorisation. Worked example: donations of £3,000 on 1 March and £3,000 on 1 September of the same year, same company and group — aggregate in the 12 months ending with the second donation is £6,000, so £1,000 of the second donation requires authorisation; had the second been £2,000 (aggregate £5,000) nothing would require authorisation, because the section bites only where the total 'exceeds' £5,000.

Step 5 — Record the consequence. Under s.378(3) an exempt donation is disregarded when determining what donations a Part 14 resolution authorises. Exemption from authorisation does not disapply any other obligation (for example declaration or register entries under Part 14 or PPERA 2000 reporting to the Electoral Commission); it is an exemption from the s.366 authorisation requirement only.

Step 6 — Note the extension. By The Unregistered Companies Regulations 2009 (S.I. 2009/2436), regs. 3–5, Sch. 1 para. 9, ss.362–379 are applied with modifications to unregistered companies (with transitional provisions and savings in regs. 7, 9 and Sch. 2). If the entity is not a company registered under the Act, check that instrument before relying on the £5,000 figure.

VERIFICATION NOTE ON THE RECORD

The harness searched the full text of the s.378 pages, the Part 14 page, the Act PDF and the contents page for '£2,000' and its variants and found none. That is a proof that the section does not state £2,000 — it is not a proof that the section states no ceiling. The section does state one, and it is £5,000, as quoted verbatim above. No figure in this note exceeds or contradicts the £5,000 ceiling stated.

This is a statement of the statutory text and how it applies, not legal advice on a specific donation; the directors should confirm the group donation history for the relevant 12-month window before making a donation.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 378 on legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2024-01-04 and 379 on legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/2026-04-06. The first reads: "378 not in force at Royal Assent see s."

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 37 on legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2024-01-04 and 378 on legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/pdfs/ukpga_20060046_en_001.pdf. The first reads: "378Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month periodU.K."

question: Y128
answer:
ANSWER

Section 586 of the Companies Act 2006 states a minimum paid-up fraction of ONE-QUARTER (25%) of the nominal value of each share allotted, plus the whole of any premium on that share. It is a per-share rule; it is not a fraction of the company's authorised minimum capital.

1. OPERATIVE TEXT (as in force on 20 November 2026)

s.586 — 'Public companies: shares must be at least one-quarter paid up'

'(1) A public company must not allot a share except as paid up at least as to one-quarter of its nominal value and the whole of any premium on it.
(2) This does not apply to shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme.
(3) If a company allots a share in contravention of this section—
   (a) the share is to be treated as if one-quarter of its nominal value, together with the whole of any premium on it, had been received, and
   (b) the allottee is liable to pay the company the minimum amount which should have been received in respect of the share under subsection (1) (less the value of any consideration actually applied in payment up, to any extent, of the share and any premium on it), with interest at the appropriate rate.
(4) Subsection (3) does not apply to the allotment of bonus shares, unless the allottee knew or ought to have known the shares were allotted in contravention of this section.'

2. VERSION CONTROL — WHY THIS IS THE TEXT 'UP TO DATE THROUGH 20 NOVEMBER 2026'

The same operative wording was read from five separate versions of the provision:
- as at 01/10/2009 (the original commencement version, also served in Welsh);
- as at 26/06/2017;
- as at 18/03/2025;
- as at 05/06/2025;
- the 'latest available' version, whose banner reads: 'Companies Act 2006, Section 586 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 22 November 2026.'

Because 20 November 2026 falls on or before the cut-off the site certifies (22 November 2026), the text quoted above is the text in force on the requested date. Two corroborating points:
(a) The only alternative version listed in the 'Changes over time' box is '01/10/2009– Amendment', i.e. the section has not been amended since commencement; the only editorial event recorded is a Correction Slip dated 15/10/2010, which is a textual correction, not a change in legal effect.
(b) The only outstanding (not-yet-applied) change listed against the provision is 'Sch. 11A para. 17E–17G substituted for Sch. 11A para. 17A–17D by 2026 c. 23 Sch. 36 para. 35' — a change to Schedule 11A, not to s.586. It therefore cannot alter the one-quarter figure.
The 'Modifications etc. (not altering text)' notes C1 and C2 (S.I. 2009/1941 art. 12(1) Sch. 3 para. 9; S.I. 2011/1265 art. 5(1) Sch. 1 para. 9) merely apply ss.584–587 to other bodies; they do not alter the fraction.

3. CORRECTION TO A COMMON MISREADING (important for compliance work)

s.586 does NOT state 'one quarter of the £50,000 authorised minimum'. The £50,000 / €65,600 figures belong to the authorised-minimum regime (s.763 and the trading-certificate provisions in Part 20; the re-registration threshold in s.91), and those provisions speak of the aggregate nominal value of allotted shares. s.586 speaks only of the paid-up fraction of each individual share. The two requirements are cumulative but independent:
- s.586: every share allotted by a plc must be at least 25% paid up on nominal value, with 100% of any premium paid up;
- authorised minimum: the plc must have allotted shares with an aggregate nominal value of at least the authorised minimum.
Consequently the sterling/euro designation question (which affects s.763) does not affect the answer to this question: the s.586 fraction is currency-neutral because it is expressed against each share's nominal value.

4. HOW TO APPLY IT (calculation)

For each share allotted by a public company, let N = nominal value and P = premium per share (P = 0 where none).
Minimum amount to be received on allotment = 0.25 × N + 1.00 × P.
Worked examples:
- £1 nominal, no premium: minimum paid up = £0.25.
- £1 nominal, £9 premium: minimum paid up = £0.25 + £9.00 = £9.25 (NOT 25% of £10 = £2.50 — the whole premium must be paid).
- £0.01 nominal, no premium: minimum paid up = £0.0025 (in practice amounts are rounded to the currency's smallest unit by the company's own allotment mechanics; the statutory floor is one-quarter).
- Nil-paid or partly paid allotments below these floors are prohibited for a plc; the same one-quarter-plus-premium floor is the reference point used in s.586(3) when the section is contravened.

5. SCOPE AND EXCEPTIONS

- Applies to public companies only (a private company is outside s.586; the equivalent constraint arises on re-registration as public).
- Carve-out: shares allotted under an employees' share scheme (s.586(2)) are exempt from the paid-up floor.
- Consequence of contravention (s.586(3)): the share is deemed to have one-quarter of nominal value plus the whole premium received, and the allottee is personally liable to the company for the shortfall plus interest at the appropriate rate.
- Bonus shares (s.586(4)): the s.586(3) consequence does not apply unless the allottee knew or ought to have known of the contravention.

6. BOTTOM LINE

Minimum paid-up fraction under s.586 CA 2006, on the text in force through 20 November 2026: one-quarter (25%) of nominal value per share, together with the whole of any premium.

The first reads: "Companies Act 2006, Section 586 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 22 November 2026."

question: Y129
answer:
MEMORANDUM

To: Requester
From: Legal
Date: 2026-11-21
Re: Word limits for motion memoranda under 16 CFR Part 3

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
Under 16 CFR Part 3, as in force on November 21, 2026, what are the word limits for memoranda supporting or opposing (a) a dispositive motion and (b) any other motion?

2. SHORT ANSWER
- A memorandum in support of, or in opposition to, a dispositive motion: 10,000 words.
- A memorandum in support of, or in opposition to, any other motion: 2,500 words.

These are the default limits in 16 CFR § 3.22(c). They apply per memorandum. They may be altered by a presiding officer/Administrative Law Judge order or a case-specific case-management order; the docket and any scheduling order should be checked in an actual proceeding.

3. GOVERNING TEXT
16 CFR § 3.22(c) states, in relevant part:

“Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any dispositive motion shall not exceed 10,000 words. Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any other motion shall not exceed 2,500 words.”

The same paragraph provides that the word-count limitation includes headings, footnotes, and quotations, but does not include the cover, table of contents, table of citations or authorities, glossaries, statements with respect to oral argument, any addendums containing statutes, rules or regulations, any certificates of counsel, proposed form of order, and any attachment required by § 3.45(e).

4. APPLICATION
(a) Dispositive motions. A dispositive motion is one seeking termination of the proceeding or of a party’s liability, such as a motion to dismiss or a motion for summary decision. The default cap for a supporting or opposing memorandum is 10,000 words. This is consistent with specific rules: § 3.31(e) independently caps memoranda supporting or opposing motions authorized by the summary-decision rule at 10,000 words, and § 3.26(e) caps memoranda supporting or opposing motions following denial of preliminary injunctive relief at 10,000 words.

(b) Any other motion. Non-dispositive or procedural motions—for example, discovery motions, motions to compel or quash, motions in limine, and similar interlocutory motions—carry a default cap of 2,500 words for a supporting or opposing memorandum.

(c) Replies are separate. Section 3.22(c) separately states that a reply in support of a dispositive motion shall not exceed 5,000 words and a reply in support of any other motion authorized by the Administrative Law Judge or the Commission shall not exceed 1,250 words. Those reply limits are not part of the “memoranda supporting or opposing” limits asked about, but they are relevant if reply briefing is contemplated.

(d) Other Part 3 word limits are not substitutes. The Commission appeal-brief limits (14,000 words for opening and answering briefs; 7,000 words for a reply brief) and the 2,500-word limit for applications for review and answers in interlocutory appeals are different filings and do not replace the motion-memorandum limits in § 3.22(c).

5. WORD-COUNT MECHANICS
Count headings, footnotes, and quotations. Do not count the cover, table of contents, table of citations or authorities, glossaries, statements with respect to oral argument, addenda containing statutes, rules or regulations, certificates of counsel, proposed form of order, or attachments required by § 3.45(e). A filing that does not comply may be refused filing or otherwise rejected under Part 3 and the presiding officer’s practice.

6. CAVEATS
These are default Part 3 limits. A specific Part 3 rule that supplies a different limit controls for that motion. A case-specific order, standing order, or ruling by the Administrative Law Judge or Commission may modify the default limits. This memorandum addresses only 16 CFR Part 3 as in force on 2026-11-21 and does not address state, other-agency, or local court rules.

7. AUTHORITY AND DATE VERIFICATION
The figures were verified against the 2026 edition of 16 CFR Part 3 and the eCFR text of § 3.22. Section 3.22 was amended at 80 FR 15160, 15161 (Mar. 23, 2015). The consulted 2026 CFR and eCFR text state the 10,000-word and 2,500-word figures for supporting or opposing motion memoranda.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10000 on ecfr.gov/current/title-16/part-3/section-3.22 and 2500 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2026-title16-vol1/pdf/cfr-2026-title16-vol1-part3.pdf. The first reads: "Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any dispositive motion shall not exceed 10,000 words."

question: Y130
answer:
MEMORANDUM — EXPIRY OF THE WITHDRAWAL PERIOD, SERVICE CONTRACT vs SALES CONTRACT
Directive 2011/83/EU (CELEX 32011L0083), Articles 9, 10, 14, 16 and Annex I(A)
Prepared for: online retailer drafting its withdrawal instructions. Scope: distance and off-premises contracts only.

=====================================================================
A. BOTTOM LINE (the answer)
=====================================================================
Both periods are 14 days. What differs is the event that starts them.

  * SERVICE CONTRACT — the withdrawal period expires 14 days after the day of the CONCLUSION OF THE CONTRACT.
    Art. 9(2)(a): 'in the case of service contracts, the day of the conclusion of the contract'.

  * SALES CONTRACT — the withdrawal period expires 14 days after the day on which the CONSUMER, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer, ACQUIRES PHYSICAL POSSESSION OF THE GOODS.
    Art. 9(2)(b), with three sub-rules:
      (i)   multiple goods ordered in one order and delivered separately -> possession of the LAST good;
      (ii)  one good delivered in multiple lots or pieces -> possession of the LAST lot or piece;
      (iii) regular delivery of goods over a defined period -> possession of the FIRST good.

  * BOTH are 'without prejudice to Article 10' (opening words of Art. 9(2)): if the trader has not given the consumer the Art. 6(1)(h) withdrawal information, the period is extended (see section E).

  * SAME RULE AS SERVICES for water/gas/electricity not put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity, district heating, and digital content not supplied on a tangible medium: trigger is the day of conclusion of the contract (Art. 9(2)(c)).

  * In no case is the rule 'order date + 14' for goods, nor 'delivery + 14' for services.

  * The right exists only for distance and off-premises contracts (Art. 9(1)), and only 'save where the exceptions provided for in Article 16 apply'. A purchase made in the shop carries no CRD withdrawal right.

=====================================================================
B. VERBATIM STATUTORY BASIS
=====================================================================
Art. 9(1): 'Save where the exceptions provided for in Article 16 apply, the consumer shall have a period of 14 days to withdraw from a distance or off-premises contract, without giving any reason, and without incurring any costs other than those provided for in Article 13(2) and Article 14.'

Art. 9(2): 'Without prejudice to Article 10, the withdrawal period referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall expire after 14 days from:
  (a) in the case of service contracts, the day of the conclusion of the contract;
  (b) in the case of sales contracts, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the goods or:
      (i)   in the case of multiple goods ordered by the consumer in one order and delivered separately, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last good;
      (ii)  in the case of delivery of a good consisting of multiple lots or pieces, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last lot or piece;
      (iii) in the case of contracts for regular delivery of goods during defined period of time, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the first good;
  (c) in the case of contracts for the supply of water, gas or electricity, where they are not put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity, of district heating or of digital content which is not supplied on a tangible medium, the day of the conclusion of the contract.'

Art. 9(3): 'The Member States shall not prohibit the contracting parties from performing their contractual obligations during the withdrawal period. Nevertheless, in the case of off-premises contracts, Member States may maintain existing national legislation prohibiting the trader from collecting the payment from the consumer during the given period after the conclusion of the contract.'

Definitions (Art. 2):
  - 'service contract' = any contract other than a sales contract under which the trader supplies or undertakes to supply a service to the consumer and the consumer pays or undertakes to pay the price.
  - 'sales contract' = any contract under which the trader transfers or undertakes to transfer ownership of goods to the consumer and the consumer pays or undertakes to pay the price, INCLUDING any contract having as its object both goods and services.

Source of the quoted text: CELEX 32011L0083 as adopted (legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2011/83/article/9/adopted and .../adopted/data.xht) and the consolidated text CELEX 02011L0083-20180701. Article 9 is worded identically in both.

=====================================================================
C. TRIGGER TABLE — WHAT TO PUT IN THE INSTRUCTIONS
=====================================================================
| Contract / delivery pattern                        | Period starts on                                             | Expires |
|----------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|---------|
| Service contract                                   | Day the contract is concluded                                | +14 days|
| Sales contract, single good                        | Day consumer (or consumer-nominated third party, not the carrier) takes physical possession | +14 days |
| Multiple goods, one order, delivered separately    | Day of possession of the LAST good                           | +14 days|
| One good delivered in several lots/pieces          | Day of possession of the LAST lot or piece                   | +14 days|
| Regular delivery over a defined period (subscription goods) | Day of possession of the FIRST good                 | +14 days|
| Water/gas/electricity not in a limited volume, district heating, digital content not on a tangible medium | Day the contract is concluded | +14 days |

Practical identification of the trigger:
  - 'Conclusion of the contract' for an online order = the moment the trader accepts the consumer's offer (in practice the order-confirmation timestamp). Fix it in the order records; the instructions should say 'the day you placed your order / we confirmed your order' only if that is genuinely the conclusion date under the applicable national contract law.
  - 'Physical possession' = actual handover to the consumer or to a person the consumer nominated (e.g. a neighbour or pick-up point designated by the consumer). Handover to the carrier is NOT the trigger; nor is handover to a pick-up point the trader chose without the consumer indicating it.

=====================================================================
D. HOW THE 14 DAYS ARE COUNTED
=====================================================================
The directive fixes the trigger event but does not itself lay down a rule for counting days; that is a matter of national law. The prevailing transposition, and the reading used by most Member States, is that the DAY OF THE TRIGGERING EVENT IS NOT COUNTED: the period runs over the following 14 days and expires at the end of the 14th day.

Worked examples (arithmetic checked):
  - Service concluded 1 March -> period expires at the end of 15 March.
  - Goods delivered 1 March -> period expires at the end of 15 March.
  - Goods delivered 10 April -> period expires at the end of 24 April.
  - Three goods ordered together, delivered 3, 9 and 17 May -> trigger is 17 May; period expires at the end of 31 May.

Two consequences to state in the instructions:
  - 'To meet the withdrawal deadline, it is sufficient for you to send your communication concerning your exercise of the right of withdrawal before the withdrawal period has expired' (Annex I(A)). The consumer does not have to have the goods back in the trader's hands by the deadline.
  - The directive does not fix a time of day; if the trader publishes one (e.g. 23:59 local time on the last day), it must not shorten the statutory period.

=====================================================================
E. THE ART. 10 EXTENSION (must be reflected in the instructions)
=====================================================================
Art. 9(2) is expressly 'without prejudice to Article 10':
  - Art. 10(1): where the trader has failed to provide the consumer with the information on the right of withdrawal required by Art. 6(1)(h), the withdrawal period expires 12 MONTHS AFTER THE END OF THE INITIAL WITHDRAWAL PERIOD.
  - Art. 10(2): if the trader supplies that information within one year from the day referred to in Art. 9(2), the period expires 14 DAYS AFTER THE DAY ON WHICH THE CONSUMER RECEIVES THAT INFORMATION.
  Maximum exposure therefore: 12 months + 14 days.
  Provenance note: the text of Art. 10 itself was not among the retrieved passages (only the cross-reference to it in Art. 9(2)); the wording above is from the directive and should be checked against the operative Art. 10 text before the instructions go to print.

Drafting consequence: the retailer's instruction template must be generated from the order data, so that the correct trigger sentence and, where relevant, the extended period are inserted automatically. A static '14 days from delivery' sentence will be wrong for services and for split deliveries.

=====================================================================
F. SERVICE-SPECIFIC RULES THE INSTRUCTIONS MUST NOT OMIT
=====================================================================
1. Early performance. The consumer may ask for the service to start inside the 14 days. Obtain (and record) the consumer's prior express request plus an acknowledgement that the right of withdrawal is lost once the service has been fully performed.
2. Loss of the right on full performance. Art. 16(a): the withdrawal right does not apply to service contracts after the service has been fully performed, if performance began with the consumer's prior express consent and the consumer acknowledged that the right is lost.
   CORRECTION TO THE WORKING ASSUMPTION: the project notes attributed this rule to Art. 16(m). Art. 16(m) is the DIGITAL-CONTENT exclusion. The correct citation for services is ART. 16(a). Art. 16(m) applies to digital content not supplied on a tangible medium where supply has begun with the consumer's prior express consent and acknowledgement of loss of the right. Both exclusions should be listed separately in the instructions.
3. Part-performance costs. Art. 14(3): where the consumer withdraws after requesting performance during the period, the consumer pays an amount proportionate to what has been supplied up to the moment of notifying the withdrawal, compared with full coverage of the contract. Art. 14(4) removes that cost in the cases it lists (e.g. where the trader failed to give the Art. 6(1)(h)/(j) information).
4. Confirmation on a durable medium. Art. 7(2)/8(7) require the trader to confirm the contract on a durable medium, including, where applicable, confirmation of the consumer's express consent and acknowledgement. Retain that record: it is the trader's evidence for refusing a late withdrawal.
5. Performance may continue during the period (Art. 9(3)); for off-premises contracts some Member States may still prohibit collecting payment during the period.

=====================================================================
G. TEXT TO INSERT — Annex I(A) MODEL INSTRUCTIONS, FILLED IN
=====================================================================
Base sentence (Annex I(A)):
  'You have the right to withdraw from this contract within 14 days without giving any reason.'

Second sentence — select ONE variant per contract type:

  SERVICE CONTRACT (and utilities not in a limited volume, district heating, digital content not on a tangible medium):
  'The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day of the conclusion of the contract.'

  SALES CONTRACT (single good):
  'The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the goods.'

  MULTIPLE GOODS ORDERED IN ONE ORDER, DELIVERED SEPARATELY:
  '... physical possession of the last good.'

  ONE GOOD DELIVERED IN MULTIPLE LOTS OR PIECES:
  '... physical possession of the last lot or piece.'

  REGULAR DELIVERY OVER A DEFINED PERIOD:
  '... physical possession of the first good.'

Closing sentences (Annex I(A)):
  'To exercise the right of withdrawal, you must inform us [trader name, postal address, e-mail address] of your decision to withdraw from this contract by an unequivocal statement (e.g. a letter sent by post, fax or e-mail). You may use the attached model withdrawal form, but it is not obligatory.'
  'To meet the withdrawal deadline, it is sufficient for you to send your communication concerning your exercise of the right of withdrawal before the withdrawal period has expired.'

Additional clause for service contracts where early performance is offered (NOT from Annex I(A) — recommended drafting, to be reviewed against national law):
  'If you want the service to begin before the 14-day withdrawal period has expired, please confirm this expressly when you place your order. You will then be asked to acknowledge that you lose your right of withdrawal once the service has been fully performed. If you withdraw after the service has begun but before it has been fully performed, you will pay an amount proportionate to the service supplied up to the moment you notify us of the withdrawal.'

=====================================================================
H. POINTS OF CAUTION AND CORRECTIONS
=====================================================================
1. FULL HARMONISATION, NOT MINIMUM HARMONISATION. The working assumption that 'the directive does not pre-empt stricter national consumer protection rules, so national law could extend or alter the periods' is WRONG for distance and off-premises contracts within the directive's scope. Art. 4 prohibits Member States from maintaining or introducing provisions diverging from the directive, save where it expressly provides otherwise. The 14 days cannot be lengthened or shortened nationally for in-scope contracts. National transposition still matters for (a) the national-language wording, (b) the day-counting rule and time of day, (c) the Art. 9(3) off-premises payment prohibition, (d) optional-scope extensions under Art. 3(2), and (e) remedies and enforcement.
2. MIXED CONTRACTS. Art. 2(5) expressly includes contracts having as their object both goods and services within 'sales contract'. Such a contract takes the sales-contract trigger (physical possession), not the day of conclusion. Do not split the period across the goods and service elements.
3. EXCEPTIONS. Art. 16 removes the right altogether for a list of goods and services (made to measure / clearly personalised goods, rapidly deteriorating goods, sealed goods unsealed after delivery where unsuitable for return on hygiene or health-protection grounds, sealed audio/video/software unsealed after delivery, newspapers/periodicals/magazines other than subscriptions, contracts concluded at public auction, accommodation/transport/car rental/catering/leisure services for a specific date or period, and others). The instructions must list the ones the retailer actually relies on; a blanket '14 days on everything' statement will be inaccurate and is an enforcement risk.
4. VERSION CONTROL. legislation.gov.uk carries the UK-retained version; for EU/EEA use the EUR-Lex text at CELEX 32011L0083 (and the consolidated 02011L0083-20180701). Art. 9 is worded identically in the adopted and 2018-consolidated texts, so the answer above does not depend on which of those two is used. Later EU amendments (Directive (EU) 2019/2161 and its application from 28 May 2022) changed information duties and penalties, not the length of the period or the Art. 9(2) triggers — verify this against the current consolidated text before publication.
5. PROVENANCE OF THIS MEMO. Sections A–D, F(2) as to Art. 16(m), and the Annex I(A) wording in section G are grounded in the retrieved text of CELEX 32011L0083 (Art. 9, Art. 2 definitions, Annex I(A) Part B, Art. 14(4)(b)). Article 10 (section E) and Article 16(a) (section F) are cited from the directive but were not among the retrieved passages and are flagged for verification against the operative text.
6. NOT COVERED: the national transposition in the Member State(s) where the retailer sells; the computation of time under the applicable national civil code; the UK Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 as they now stand domestically. These should be checked by local counsel before the instructions are published, but none of them changes the answer to the question asked here.

question: Y131
answer:
# Answer — the presumption applicable to everyone charged with a criminal offence

## 1. Verbatim text (English official version)

> **Article 6 § 2 — Right to a fair trial (European Convention on Human Rights)**
>
> "Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law."

This is the presumption of innocence. It is the only provision in the Convention that states a presumption applicable to "everyone charged with a criminal offence". Reproduce it character-for-character: capital "E" at the start, "proved" (not "proven"), "according to law" (not "in accordance with law"), full stop at the end, no quotation marks inside the sentence.

## 2. Citation block for the training module

- Instrument: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (European Convention on Human Rights), as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15 and supplemented by Protocols Nos. 1, 4, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 16.
- Provision: Article 6 (Right to a fair trial), paragraph 2.
- Language: English (official, authentic). The same publication states: "Only the English and French versions of the Convention are authentic."
- Source cited: Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights official text, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_eng (retrieved 22 November 2026; document sha256 f4608f7ed2d5).
- Status of text: the same publication states that "The text of the Convention is presented as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) as from its entry into force on 1 June 2010." This is therefore the text as presented through Protocol No. 15.
- Suggested footnote form: Eur. Convention on Human Rights, Art. 6 § 2, as presented in the text amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15 (Council of Europe/ECHR official English version, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_eng).

## 3. Handling the "as amended through Protocol No. 15" qualifier — why the wording is unchanged

The module can state, accurately and with a source, that Protocol No. 15 does not touch Article 6 at all. Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213), by its own operative articles as published (https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Protocol_15_ENG):

- Article 1 — adds a new recital to the Preamble (subsidiarity / margin of appreciation);
- Article 2 — inserts a new paragraph 2 in Article 21 and renumbers; deletes Article 23 § 2 and renumbers;
- Article 3 — deletes the words "unless one of the parties to the case objects" in Article 30;
- Article 4 — in Article 35 § 1, replaces "within a period of six months" with "within a period of four months";
- Article 5 — deletes a sub-paragraph of Article 35 § 3 (b).

No operative article of Protocol No. 15 refers to Article 6. Protocol No. 15 entered into force on 1 August 2021 (ECHR protocols page, https://www.echr.coe.int/protocols: "Protocol No. 15 entered into force on 1 August 2021, all the member States of the Council of Europe having ratified it"). Consequence for the module: the Article 6 § 2 sentence quoted above is identical before and after Protocol No. 15; the qualifier affects the surrounding text (Preamble, Articles 21, 23, 30, 35), not this sentence. Say this explicitly rather than implying Protocol No. 15 rewrote the presumption.

## 4. Teaching context — surrounding paragraphs (for placement, not as the answer)

Article 6 § 2 sits inside the fair-trial article; keep the distinction from its neighbours clear:

- **Article 6 § 1** (scope/fair hearing): "In the determination of his civil rights and obligations or of any criminal charge against him, everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. ..."
- **Article 6 § 2** (the presumption — the answer): "Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law."
- **Article 6 § 3** (minimum rights, distinct from the presumption): "Everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights: (a) to be informed promptly, in a language which he understands and in detail, of the nature and cause of the accusation against him; (b) to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence; (c) to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing or, if he has not sufficient means to pay for legal assistance, to be given it free when the interests of justice so require; (d) to examine or have examined witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him; (e) to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court."

Note for trainers: § 3 rights are commonly confused with § 2; the presumption is § 2 only, and § 2 is not one of the "minimum rights" listed in § 3.

## 5. Copy-paste block for the module

```
Article 6 § 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights (text as presented
as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15, in force for Protocol No. 15
from 1 August 2021):

"Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent
until proved guilty according to law."

Source: Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights, official English
version, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_eng
```

## 6. Drafting and accuracy rules for the module

1. Quote, never paraphrase: no "presumption of innocence until proven guilty", no "innocent until proven guilty", no "presumed innocent until proven guilty". The Convention's own words are "shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law".
2. Keep "proved", not "proven" — the authentic English text uses "proved".
3. Keep "charged with a criminal offence" — not "accused of a crime", not "defendant".
4. Do not import the Article 6 § 1 wording ("any criminal charge against him") into § 2; they are different formulations in the same article.
5. Do not attach the phrase "presumption of innocence" to the quotation as if it were the treaty wording; it is the standard doctrinal label for the right, and may be used in commentary clearly outside the quotation marks.
6. Language: the English version is authentic, but it is authentic jointly with the French. If the module is bilingual or a French quotation is required, take the French text from the official French version of the same publication rather than translating the English — only the English and French texts are authentic, and a translation would not be. The French official text is NOT reproduced here because the French page was not retrieved for this work; obtain it from the ECHR official texts page before printing it.
7. Pin the source: cite the ECHR official text URL and the retrieval date in the module's source list, so the quotation can be re-verified.

## 7. Note on the absence-of-string check

The harness's absence check on https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_eng searched for the strings "presumption of innocence", "innocent until proven guilty", "presumption of innocence until proven guilty", "innocence presumption", and "presumption of innocence (ECHR Art. 6(2))". Those five strings are paraphrases or labels; none of them is the Convention's operative wording. The page does state the answer, in the words "Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law", which the same fetch extracted as a passage. The absence of the five paraphrase strings therefore does not amount to the page stating none, and ask 1 is not reported as not stated. The absence check is itself a useful teaching point: searching a treaty for a doctrinal label can return nothing while the provision sits plainly in the text under different words.

## 8. Source-quality notes (for the module's source list)

- https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_eng — used and quoted; official English text as amended through Protocol No. 15.
- https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Protocol_15_ENG — used to confirm which articles Protocol No. 15 amends (none of them Article 6).
- https://www.echr.coe.int/protocols — used to confirm Protocol No. 15's entry into force on 1 August 2021.
- https://fra.europa.eu/en/law-reference/european-convention-human-rights-article-6 — not usable: the fetch returned a bot-verification interstitial, not the legal text. Do not cite.
- https://ks.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr-ks/guide_art_15_eng-pdf — not relevant to Article 6; it is the case-law guide on Article 15 (derogation in time of emergency). Do not cite for the presumption.
- HUDOC press-release page on Protocol No. 15's entry into force — not used for the wording; the treaty text itself is the source of the quotation.

question: Y132
answer:
Under 16 CFR Part 3 as shown in the grounding (2026 CFR / eCFR text, operative for 2026-11-21), the two stated periods are:

1. Answer period — 16 CFR § 3.12(a): 'A respondent shall file an answer within 14 days after being served with the complaint.'
2. Scheduling conference period — 16 CFR § 3.21(b): 'Not later than 10 days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent, the Administrative Law Judge shall hold a scheduling conference.'

In a single-respondent adjudication, the respondent is the 'last answering respondent.' If the respondent uses the entire answer period, the answer is filed on day 14 after service. If the ALJ then uses the entire post-answer period, the scheduling conference is held on day 24 after service: 14 days + 10 days = 24 days.

Therefore, the combined interval from service of the complaint to the scheduling conference is 24 days.

This uses only the two stated periods, as requested. No tolling, extension, or intervening procedural step is added. The day of service is not counted in the 14-day answer period, and the day the answer is filed is not counted in the 10-day conference period; the arithmetic remains 14 + 10 = 24 days. No weekend or holiday adjustment is applied because the request limits the calculation to the two stated periods and supplies no service date; such an adjustment would affect the calendar date, not the stated-period sum.

The proof of absence for ask 1 is consistent with this result: section 3.21 does not state a 60-day interval, and the searched strings ('60 days', 'sixty days', etc.) are absent. Section 3.21 states the 10-day post-answer period, and § 3.12(a) supplies the 14-day answer period.
cautions: The answer gives 24 days for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: Y133
answer:
# Threshold-excess calculation — Article 1(2)(a)–(b), Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004

## 1. Legal basis and thresholds applied

Source text (OJ 29.1.2004 L 24, as reproduced in the EUR-Lex / WIPO Lex copies of the Regulation):

- Article 1(2)(a): "the combined aggregate worldwide turnover of all the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 5 000 million; and"
- Article 1(2)(b): "the aggregate Community-wide turnover of each of at least two of the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 250 million"

Thresholds applied in this calculation: **EUR 5,000 million** (combined aggregate worldwide) and **EUR 250 million** (aggregate Community-wide, applied per undertaking). These are the figures in the Regulation as adopted; no later amendment to the Article 1(2) amounts has been applied, and no national or member-state threshold figure enters this calculation.

Source note: the legislation.gov.uk copy of the Regulation is the version revoked for the UK (S.I. 2019/93, Sch. 3 para. 1(g); 2020 c. 1, Sch. 5 para. 1(1)) with Article 1 omitted from the revised text. It is not used. The EU text is the operative authority for the arithmetic.

## 2. Method

For each recorded amount: **excess = recorded amount − corresponding threshold**.

The provision uses "more than", i.e. a strict inequality. An excess must therefore be strictly positive for the recorded amount to be above the threshold; an excess of zero would mean the figure sits *at* the threshold and not above it. All excesses below are strictly positive.

Each recorded amount is matched to its own provision. The mapping is not interchangeable and the figures are not pooled:

| Recorded amount (EUR million) | Corresponding provision | Corresponding threshold (EUR million) |
|---|---|---|
| 5,400 (combined aggregate worldwide) | Art 1(2)(a) | 5,000 |
| 300 (Community-wide, undertaking 1) | Art 1(2)(b) | 250 |
| 275 (Community-wide, undertaking 2) | Art 1(2)(b) | 250 |

**Critical point on Article 1(2)(b):** the EUR 300 million and EUR 275 million figures are each tested against the EUR 250 million figure **separately**. They are not added together (which would give 575) and are not tested against any single aggregate Community-wide threshold. Article 1(2)(b) is a per-undertaking test. Aggregating the two would be a category error and is not done here.

## 3. Computation

1. **Combined aggregate worldwide turnover (Art 1(2)(a))**
   5,400 − 5,000 = **EUR 400 million** above the threshold.

2. **Community-wide turnover, undertaking 1 (Art 1(2)(b))**
   300 − 250 = **EUR 50 million** above the threshold.

3. **Community-wide turnover, undertaking 2 (Art 1(2)(b))**
   275 − 250 = **EUR 25 million** above the threshold.

| Amount tested | Provision | Recorded | Threshold | Excess |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Combined aggregate worldwide | Art 1(2)(a) | EUR 5,400 m | EUR 5,000 m | **EUR 400 m** |
| Community-wide, undertaking 1 | Art 1(2)(b) | EUR 300 m | EUR 250 m | **EUR 50 m** |
| Community-wide, undertaking 2 | Art 1(2)(b) | EUR 275 m | EUR 250 m | **EUR 25 m** |

Strict-inequality check: 400 > 0, 50 > 0, 25 > 0. Each recorded amount is strictly above its own threshold; none is at or below it. No figure is at the margin in the sense of equality with a threshold.

## 4. Precision and units

- Unit: millions of euros (EUR million), nominal, as recorded.
- No currency conversion and no deflator or indexation adjustment is applied.
- All inputs are whole millions, so the subtractions are exact and no rounding convention is needed; the results are reported to the same precision as the inputs (whole EUR million).
- If a filing template requires thousands of euros: EUR 400,000 thousand / EUR 50,000 thousand / EUR 25,000 thousand.

## 5. What this calculation does NOT decide (constraint observed)

This memorandum stops at arithmetic. It expresses **no view on whether the concentration has a Community dimension**, and nothing below is assessed:

- whether the "unless" clause of Article 1(2) is satisfied (each undertaking concerned achieving more than two-thirds of its aggregate Community-wide turnover within one and the same Member State);
- the alternative thresholds in Article 1(3) (which use different figures, EUR 2,500 million / EUR 100 million — outside the requested Article 1(2)(a)–(b) check and not applied here, with no excess computed against them);
- referral mechanisms (Article 4(4)–(5), Article 9, Article 22) and the Article 1(4) member-state request provisions;
- the correct turnover perimeter under Article 5 (associated undertakings, acquisition of parts, etc.). The recorded figures are taken as given, exactly as the request supplies them.

An arithmetic excess over the Article 1(2) thresholds is necessary but not sufficient for a Community dimension. No conclusion on that question is stated, and none should be inferred from this table.

## 6. Answer in one line

Against EUR 5,000 million the recorded EUR 5,400 million exceeds by **EUR 400 million**; against EUR 250 million the recorded EUR 300 million exceeds by **EUR 50 million** and the recorded EUR 275 million exceeds by **EUR 25 million** — each comparison being made per undertaking as Article 1(2)(b) requires.

question: Y134
answer:
LEGAL ANALYSIS — Directive 2011/83/EU, Article 3(4) optional off-premises exclusion, EUR 50 threshold, aggregation of related contracts

1. Question presented
A Member State has adopted the optional exclusion in Article 3(4) of Directive 2011/83/EU at the maximum permitted value of EUR 50. A consumer simultaneously concludes two off-premises contracts with related subject matter, requiring payments of EUR 30 and EUR 25. Two questions follow: (i) what total is used for the threshold; and (ii) does the optional exclusion cover this pair on that basis?

2. Governing text
Article 3(4) of Directive 2011/83/EU provides: 'Member States may decide not to apply this Directive or not to maintain or introduce corresponding national provisions to off-premises contracts for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50. Member States may define a lower value in their national legislation.'

Recital 28 provides: 'In order to avoid administrative burden being placed on traders, Member States may decide not to apply this Directive where goods or services of a minor value are sold off-premises. The monetary threshold should be established at a sufficiently low level as to exclude only purchases of small significance. Member States should be allowed to define this value in their national legislation provided that it does not exceed EUR 50. Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.'

The aggregation rule is expressed in Recital 28, not in the operative text of Article 3(4). It is the only expression of the aggregation rule in the Directive and is the interpretive guide to Article 3(4). A Directive-conforming reading of Article 3(4) therefore requires the threshold to be applied to the aggregated total where the conditions in Recital 28 are met.

3. Application
Three conditions in Recital 28 must be satisfied: (a) two or more contracts; (b) with related subjects; (c) concluded at the same time by the consumer.

(a) Two contracts: the premise states two contracts. If in fact the two documents were a single contract split into two documents, the result is the same — a single payment obligation of EUR 55 — so the conclusion is stable across that characterisation.
(b) Related subjects: the premise stipulates related subject matter. This is ultimately a factual and characterisation question for the national court or authority, but on the stipulated facts the condition is met.
(c) At the same time: the premise states the contracts were concluded simultaneously.

Calculation: EUR 30 + EUR 25 = EUR 55.

The threshold is EUR 50, adopted at the maximum permitted value. The statutory test is whether the payment 'does not exceed EUR 50'. The boundary is inclusive: a total of exactly EUR 50 would be within the exclusion. EUR 55 is above EUR 50. Therefore the optional exclusion does not cover the pair on the aggregation basis.

4. Answers
Ask 1 — total used for the threshold: EUR 55.
Ask 2 — does the optional exclusion cover this pair on that basis: No. The exclusion does not apply, because the aggregated total of EUR 55 exceeds the EUR 50 maximum threshold.

5. Consequences
Because the Article 3(4) exclusion is not available, the two off-premises contracts remain within the Directive's scope (subject to any other applicable exclusion in Article 3(3) and to national law). The consumer therefore retains the Directive's off-premises protections, including the pre-contractual information requirements in Article 6 and the right of withdrawal in Article 9, as transposed.

6. Qualifications a national court or authority would examine
(a) Operative basis of aggregation. Recital 28 is a recital, not an operative article. A national transposition that omitted the aggregation rule could, on a literal national-law reading, produce a different result. The correct approach is a Directive-conforming interpretation of the national provision, reading it together with Recital 28. If the national measure is incapable of such an interpretation, its conformity with the Directive would need to be examined.
(b) 'Related subjects'. This is a factual test turning on the content and commercial purpose of the two contracts. The answer above assumes the stipulated relatedness. If the contracts were genuinely unrelated, each would be assessed separately: EUR 30 and EUR 25 are each at or below EUR 50, so each would fall within the exclusion. That is the only characterisation that changes the outcome.
(c) Composition of the payment. The test is the payment to be made by the consumer. If either EUR 30 or EUR 25 includes ancillary charges (delivery, payment fees, taxes) that national law treats differently, the aggregated figure could change. On the premise that these are the consumers' payment obligations for the contracts, the figure is EUR 55.
(d) Member State's chosen value. The premise fixes the maximum of EUR 50. A Member State that had defined a lower value would have a lower threshold and the same conclusion (exclusion inapplicable) would follow a fortiori.

7. Conclusion
The total used for the threshold is EUR 55. Because EUR 55 exceeds the EUR 50 maximum threshold, the optional off-premises-contract exclusion does not cover this pair on the aggregation basis.
cautions: The recompute vote worded ask 2 differently from this answer; a decision model judged the two to say the same thing.
The answer gives 55 EUR for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: Y135
answer:
MEMORANDUM — STATUS OF THE FRCP APPENDIX OF FORMS AND THE EFFECTIVE DATE OF ITS CHANGE

I. SHORT ANSWER

1. Status (ask 1): ABROGATED. In the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as amended to December 1, 2025, there is no operative Appendix of Forms. Title XII, "APPENDIX OF FORMS," appears only as a stub reading "[Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" The enabling rule, Rule 84 ("Forms"), was abrogated in the same package and appears as "Rule 84. Abrogated, eff. Dec. 1, 2015."

2. Effective date (ask 2): DECEMBER 1, 2015. The change was made by the Supreme Court's order of April 29, 2015, transmitted to Congress under 28 U.S.C. § 2072, and took effect on December 1, 2015. April 29, 2015 is the order/transmittal date, not the effective date; do not use it as the operative date.

3. The December 1, 2025 amendments did not touch this. The abrogation predates them by ten years and remains in force; the current text "as amended to December 1, 2025" still shows Title XII as abrogated.

II. AUTHORITY RELIED ON

A. Supreme Court order, April 29, 2015 (supremecourt.gov, "frcv15(update)_1823.pdf").
   - "ORDERED: 1. That the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure be, and they hereby are, amended by including therein amendments to Civil Rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, 55, and 84, and the Appendix of Forms."
   - "2. That the foregoing amendments to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure shall take effect on December 1, 2015, and shall govern in all proceedings in civil cases thereafter commenced and, insofar as just and practicable, all proceedings then pending."
   - Transmitted text: "Rule 84. Forms [Abrogated (Apr. __, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" and "APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. __, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" (The blank day in the transmitted text is the placeholder in the proposed amendments; the order itself is dated April 29, 2015.)

B. Federal Judicial Center, amendments page for Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 (fjc.gov).
   - "Amendments to the following Federal Rules of Civil Procedure became effective on December 1, 2015: 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55. Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms were abrogated."
   - Companion entry: "Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Transmittal to Congress, April 29, 2015."

C. Legal Information Institute, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure index (law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp), expressly "as amended to December 1, 2025."
   - "Rule 84. Abrogated, eff. Dec. 1, 2015"
   - "XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]"

Source caveat: the uscourts.gov FRCP landing page does not itself mention the Appendix of Forms and does not contain the string "December 1, 2025"; it says only that "[t]he Civil Rules were last amended in 2025" and links the "Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Pamphlet, Dec. 1, 2025." The answer therefore rests on the three sources above (A–C), not on that landing page.

III. CHRONOLOGY (each date labeled by its role)

- April 29, 2015 — date of the Supreme Court order amending Rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, 55, and 84 and the Appendix of Forms; transmitted to Congress under 28 U.S.C. § 2072.
- December 1, 2015 — EFFECTIVE DATE of those amendments, including the abrogation of Rule 84 and of the Appendix of Forms. This is the date the change took effect.
- December 1, 2025 — date through which the current rules text is amended; the Appendix of Forms remains abrogated as of that date. No 2025 amendment revived, replaced, or renumbered it.

IV. WHAT THE STATUS IS NOT (negative findings, to prevent miscitation)

- Not "superseded" or "renumbered." Abrogation removed Title XII and Rule 84 outright; there is no successor appendix and no new rule number to which the old forms were moved.
- Not a 2025 change. Nothing in the 2025 amendment cycle is the source; a manual updated to 2025 must still record the 2015 abrogation.
- Not a statutory repeal by Congress. The change came through the Rules Enabling Act process (Supreme Court order, transmitted to Congress, effective absent contrary congressional action).
- Not to be confused with other form sets. The Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure forms, the Bankruptcy Official Forms, and the court's AO forms are separate instruments and were not affected by this abrogation.

V. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE 2014 MANUAL (practice consequences)

The manual's direction to "see the Appendix of Forms" is now a dead reference. Consequences to build into the update:

1. Every citation of the form "Fed. R. Civ. P. Form __" (e.g., Form 11, Form 18, Form 52) is obsolete as a rule citation. Form 18 (complaint for negligence) in particular should not be cited as supplying a pleading standard; the model-form safe harbor it represented is gone.
2. The substantive content did not vanish from practice — it migrated to the Administrative Office forms and to the rules themselves. Practical substitutes practitioners now use (confirm each against uscourts.gov before relying on it in the manual):
   - Summons — AO 440.
   - Waiver of the Service of Summons — AO 398; Notice of a Lawsuit and Request to Waive Service — AO 399.
   - Civil Cover Sheet — JS 44.
   - Subpoena — AO 88A / AO 88B.
   - Judgment — AO 450.
   These are court forms, not rule text; cite them as AO/JS forms, not as FRCP forms.
3. Local practice: many districts maintain their own forms and local rules on service, default judgment, and scheduling. The manual should add a step telling users to check the district's local rules and website, because after abrogation there is no single national form set in the FRCP to fall back on.
4. Broader review: a 2014 manual is now at least eleven years stale. Beyond this one reference, audit for (a) the 2015 amendments to Rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55 (including the discovery proportionality and preservation changes), (b) later amendment cycles through December 1, 2025, and (c) any reliance on model forms as statements of governing law.

VI. REPLACEMENT DRAFTING LANGUAGE FOR THE MANUAL

Delete: "See the Appendix of Forms to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure for the applicable form."

Substitute: "The Appendix of Forms to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure was abrogated effective December 1, 2015 (Supreme Court order of April 29, 2015; Rule 84 abrogated in the same order). There are no longer official forms appended to the Civil Rules. For national forms, use the Administrative Office forms available at uscourts.gov (e.g., AO 440 Summons; AO 398/399 waiver of service; JS 44 Civil Cover Sheet). Check the local rules and the district court's website for any district-specific form requirements."

VII. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST FOR THE REVIEWER

1. Open the current FRCP text as amended to December 1, 2025 and confirm Title XII reads "APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" and Rule 84 reads "Abrogated, eff. Dec. 1, 2015."
2. Confirm the effective date, December 1, 2015, in the Supreme Court order of April 29, 2015 (paragraph 2 of the ORDERED clauses), not from the order's date line.
3. Confirm that the December 1, 2025 pamphlet carries the abrogation forward unchanged.
4. Confirm no local rule in the relevant district re-adopts FRCP form numbering.

VIII. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE TWO ASKS

- Ask 1 — status: abrogated (Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms, abrogated by the Supreme Court order of April 29, 2015).
- Ask 2 — effective date of the change: December 1, 2015.

question: Y136
answer:
CORRECTION MEMORANDUM — TRAINING SLIDE: ECtHR JUDGES' TERMS OF OFFICE
Prepared: 22 November 2026 | Governing text: ECHR as amended by Protocols No. 14 and No. 15 (English version)

1. BOTTOM LINE
1.1 The election term is NINE YEARS (9).
1.2 A judge MAY NOT be re-elected. The term is a single, non-renewable term.
1.3 The slide's statement ('renewable six-year terms') is WRONG as a statement of current law. It describes the regime that ceased to apply to judges elected from 1 June 2010 onwards. The error originates in Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94), not in Protocol No. 15 — Protocol No. 15 did not alter the length or the renewability of the term at all.

2. CONTROLLING PROVISION AND EXACT WORDING
2.1 Provision: Article 23 (Terms of office and dismissal), paragraph 1, of the Convention as amended.
2.2 Verbatim (numbered-article format, ETS 5 consolidated text, https://rm.coe.int/1680a2353d, sha256 ba0fe36805b8):
    "Article 23 – Terms of office and dismissal
     1  The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
     2  The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration."
2.3 Verbatim (ECHR official text presented as amended by Protocol No. 15, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_Watermark_P15_ENG, sha256 cc3ebf842b81):
    "ARTICLE 23 — Terms of office and dismissal
     1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
     2. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration."
2.4 Third, corroborating official quotation (PACE/Secretary General guidance on the election procedure, SG-AS (2026) 01, https://rm.coe.int/procedure-for-the-election-of-judges-to-the-european-court-of-human-ri/1680aa8ddf, sha256 449564d229b2, para. 13): "Article 23 of the Convention, as amended by Protocol No. 15 to the Convention, stipulates: '1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected. 2. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration.'"
2.5 Election mechanism (context, unchanged): Article 22 — judges are elected by the Parliamentary Assembly, in respect of each High Contracting Party, by a majority of votes cast, from a list of three candidates nominated by that Party. Article 23 §1 fixes the term; Article 22 fixes the manner of election. The two must be cited together in any corrected slide.

3. ANSWERS TO THE TWO QUESTIONS ASKED
3.1 'What is the election term?' — Nine years. Article 23 §1, first sentence. (Results entry: ask 1 = 9 years.)
3.2 'May a judge be re-elected?' — No. Article 23 §1, second sentence: 'They may not be re-elected.' Note for accuracy in the slide: Article 25 §1(a) and (c) do allow re-election, but only of the President/Vice-Presidents and of Chamber Presidents in their institutional capacities — not of judges to the Court. Do not let that coincidence of wording be misread as permitting a judge's re-election; it concerns internal office-holders, not the judicial mandate.

4. WHY THE SLIDE IS WRONG (DIAGNOSIS, FOR THE TRAINER'S NOTE)
4.1 Pre-1 June 2010 regime: judges were elected for a renewable six-year term. That is the source of the slide's wording.
4.2 Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94) replaced this with a single nine-year term. The ECHR 'Protocols' page states that the measures in Protocol No. 14 include 'changing the judges' term of office to a single, nine year term' (https://www.echr.coe.int/protocols, sha256 35fce35b4cec). Protocol No. 14 entered into force on 1 June 2010 — recited on the face of the amended Convention: 'The text of the Convention is presented as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94) as from its entry into force on 1 June 2010.'
4.3 Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213), in force 1 August 2021, did NOT change Article 23 §1's term or the bar on re-election. Its effects on judges' terms were indirect:
    (a) it deleted the former Article 23 §2, which had provided that a judge's term expired on reaching the age of 70 (SG-AS (2026) 01, footnote 26: 'Former paragraph 2 of Article 23 ("The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70") was deleted by Protocol 15');
    (b) it inserted a new Article 21 §2: 'Candidates shall be less than 65 years of age at the date by which the list of three candidates has been requested by the Parliamentary Assembly, further to Article 22.'
    The Protocol No. 15 explanatory report confirms the linkage: the change was intended 'to enable highly qualified judges to serve the full nine-year term of office', and the age limit was 'no longer essential ... given the fact that judges' terms of office are no longer renewable' (https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng, sha256 d85a250bb703, paras 11–12). Note the premise: nine years, non-renewable — i.e. the Protocol 14 rule is treated as settled background by Protocol 15.
4.4 Conclusion for the slide: the error is a regime-confusion error of roughly sixteen years' standing, not a Protocol 15 point. Any trainer's note should say so explicitly, because a reviewer who checks only Protocol 15 will find nothing in it about six years and may wrongly conclude the slide is fine.

5. TRANSITIONAL PROVISIONS — CAVEAT TO STATE, NOT TO OVERSTATE
5.1 Transitional rules can make old-law statements true of individual judges without being true of the Convention text. Protocol No. 15's own transitional provision (Article 8 §1) applies the Article 21 §2 age criterion only to judges elected from lists submitted after entry into force; judges on previously submitted lists, including judges in office and judges-elect at 1 August 2021, remain subject to the pre-existing rule (expiry at 70) — explanatory report, para. 15.
5.2 Protocol No. 14 likewise carried transitional arrangements for judges elected before its entry into force. I have NOT re-verified the verbatim text of Protocol No. 14's transitional article in this exercise and therefore do not quote or paraphrase it. If the training audience includes judges elected before 1 June 2010, obtain the text of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94) and its explanatory report before asserting which individual mandates ran on the six-year renewable basis.
5.3 The safe formulation for the slide: 'Judges are elected for a single, non-renewable nine-year term (Article 23 §1). Mandates begun under the pre-1 June 2010 six-year renewable regime continued under the rules applicable at the time of election.'

6. DROP-IN REPLACEMENT TEXT FOR THE SLIDE
6.1 Headline (replaces 'renewable six-year terms'):
    "Judges of the European Court of Human Rights are elected for a single term of nine years. They may not be re-elected."
6.2 Citation line (place under the headline, small type):
    "ECHR, Article 23 §1, as amended by Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94, in force 1 June 2010) and presented as amended by Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213, in force 1 August 2021)."
6.3 Optional supporting bullet: "Judges are elected by the Parliamentary Assembly from a list of three candidates nominated by the State concerned (Article 22). They hold office until replaced and continue to deal with cases already under consideration (Article 23 §2). Candidates must be under 65 at the date the list of three is requested (Article 21 §2, inserted by Protocol No. 15)."
6.4 Historical footnote, if the deck keeps an 'evolution' panel: "Until 1 June 2010 judges served renewable six-year terms; Protocol No. 14 replaced this with a single nine-year term."

7. EVIDENCE TABLE (what each source establishes)
7.1 https://rm.coe.int/1680a2353d (ETS 5 consolidated, sha256 ba0fe36805b8, fetched 2026-11-22): Article 23 §1 text; Article 22; Article 21; footnote recording that the Article 21/23 amendments take effect under Protocol No. 15 from 1 August 2021.
7.2 https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_Watermark_P15_ENG (sha256 cc3ebf842b81, fetched 2026-11-22): same Article 23 §1 text; express statement that the text is presented as amended by Protocols No. 15 (from 1 August 2021) and No. 14 (from 1 June 2010); 'Entry into force: 01/08/2021'.
7.3 https://rm.coe.int/procedure-for-the-election-of-judges-to-the-european-court-of-human-ri/1680aa8ddf (SG-AS (2026) 01, sha256 449564d229b2, fetched 2026-11-22): quotes Article 23 §§1–2 as amended by Protocol No. 15; confirms deletion of the former Article 23 §2 age-70 rule; describes commencement of the nine-year term.
7.4 https://www.echr.coe.int/protocols (sha256 35fce35b4cec, fetched 2026-11-22): Protocol No. 14 'changing the judges' term of office to a single, nine year term' — the bridge between the slide's six-year claim and the current text.
7.5 https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng (sha256 d85a250bb703, fetched 2026-11-22): paras 11–15 — purpose of the new Article 21 §2, deletion of the age limit, and the transitional rule in Article 8 §1.

8. DISCLOSURE: PROOF OF ABSENCE ON ONE PAGE, AND WHY IT DOES NOT CONTROL
8.1 The harness holds a proof of absence for ask 1 in respect of https://search.coe.int/cm/eng?i=091259488028055b (1,750 characters, sha256 158056c349fc): none of 'term', 'mandate', 'duration', 'period', 'six years', '6 yr', '6-year term' appears anywhere in its full text.
8.2 That finding is correct and irrelevant to the answer: the page is a Committee of Ministers search/landing page, not a text of the Convention. It states nothing about judges' terms, and nothing in this memorandum relies on it. Because the ask is answered — expressly, and in three independent official sources — this is not a case in which 'the page states none' is the answer to the question, so ask 1 is not recorded as not stated.
8.3 Conversely, no part of the answer rests on inference from silence. Article 23 §1 states both the term and the bar on re-election in terms.

9. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS OF THIS ADVICE
9.1 The English version is treated as controlling (per the project assumption). Other language versions were not compared; a divergence check is unnecessary for a training slide in English but should be run before the wording is used in any multilingual or legally operative document.
9.2 Article 23 §1 as quoted is the Convention text; the Court's internal organisation (Presidents, Registrar, Chamber Presidents, Article 25) is expressly outside this answer except for the warning at 3.2.
9.3 Edge case flagged, not resolved: the position of a judge who leaves office before completing a nine-year term and is later proposed again. 'They may not be re-elected' bars re-election to the Court; whether a fresh election after an incomplete mandate is legally possible is a question on which specific advice should be taken from the Registry/PACE Secretariat before it is asserted in training material. It does not affect the two answers given.
9.4 If the deck also states the application time-limit or other Protocol No. 15 changes, note for the reviewer that Protocol No. 15 reduced the time-limit from six to four months (ECHR 'Protocols' page). That 'six' is a different six from the slide's term error and must not be conflated when the deck is corrected.

10. VERDICT
10.1 Ask 1: election term = 9 years. Re-election: not permitted (Article 23 §1, ECHR as amended through Protocol No. 15).
10.2 The slide must be corrected, not merely annotated: replace 'renewable six-year terms' with 'a single, non-renewable nine-year term', cite Article 23 §1, and — if the historical regime is retained for teaching purposes — label it expressly as pre-1 June 2010 law superseded by Protocol No. 14.

question: Y137
answer:
ANSWER
1. No. A State-aid team cannot rely on Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 (GBER) to exempt aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine from the Article 108(3) TFEU notification obligation. That category is expressly excluded from the GBER's scope.

2. The instrument identified by the GBER's scope passage is Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24). The Regulation cites it as 'Council Decision No 2010/787' in Article 1(3)(d) and as 'Council Decision 2010/787/EU' in the consolidated text.

TEXTUAL BASIS
- GBER Article 1(3) provides: 'This Regulation shall not apply to: ... (d) aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, as covered by Council Decision No 2010/787'. The same exclusion appears in the original and consolidated versions; the consolidated 2020 text reads 'as covered by Council Decision 2010/787/EU'.
- GBER Recital 12 states: 'This Regulation should not apply to aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, which is dealt with by the Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines. This Regulation should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid.'
- GBER Article 2(13) defines 'coal' by reference to the same Council decision of 10 December 2010, confirming that the closure-aid category is governed by that instrument rather than by the GBER.

LEGAL EFFECT
- The GBER is a block-exemption instrument: aid must fall within its material and personal scope before any exemption from notification can operate. Because Article 1(3)(d) places closure aid for uncompetitive coal mines outside the GBER's scope, no GBER article can supply the exemption. The notification duty in Article 108(3) TFEU therefore remains unless another applicable instrument covers the measure.
- The exclusion is category-specific. It is not a blanket exclusion of all coal-sector aid: Recital 12 states that the GBER should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, except regional aid. The carve-out is for aid 'to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines'.
- The identified instrument is Council Decision 2010/787/EU. Whether a particular measure can be granted without individual notification, and on what conditions, must be assessed under that Decision and its own procedural and temporal provisions, not under the GBER. The Decision is time-limited (it applied until 31 December 2018 under its own terms, subject to its provisions); its temporal validity must be checked for the grant date in question. If the Decision no longer applies, the GBER carve-out still prevents reliance on the GBER, and the measure would need to be assessed directly against the Treaty and notification rules.

ON THE PROOF OF ABSENCE
- I do not enter ask 2 in not_stated. The harness's proof of absence searched for strings such as 'Coal Mine Closure Aid (CMCA)', 'Coal Mine Closure Instrument (CMCI)', 'Coal Mine Closure Scheme', etc. Those are not the designation used by Regulation 651/2014. The fetched page expressly contains 'Council Decision No 2010/787' in Article 1(3)(d), and the recital on the same page names the 'Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines'. The answer is therefore stated in the grounding, not absent from it.
