question: Y152
answer:
ANSWER TO ASK 1 (VERDICT: NO)

Apart from § 248.30(b), 17 CFR Part 248, Subpart A does not cover information about companies, and does not cover information about individuals who obtain financial products or services primarily for business purposes. The exclusion is express in the text of the subpart, not inferred.

1. OPERATIVE TEXT

17 CFR § 248.1(b) (scope), quoted verbatim from the eCFR Subpart A page (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-248/subpart-A, fetched 2026-11-23T00:25:28Z, sha256 d91a3c8df350; same sentence also quoted at https://ecfr.gov/current/title-17/part-248/subpart-A and https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-248):

  "Except with respect to § 248.30(b), this subpart applies only to nonpublic personal information about individuals who obtain financial products or services primarily for personal, family, or household purposes from the institutions listed below. This subpart does not apply to information about companies or about individuals who obtain financial products or services primarily for business, commercial, or agricultural purposes."

Two operative consequences follow directly:
  (a) Subject-matter limit — the subpart reaches only nonpublic personal information about individuals acting for personal, family, or household purposes.
  (b) Express exclusion — information about companies, and information about individuals whose products/services are primarily for business, commercial, or agricultural purposes, is outside the subpart.
  (c) Sole carve-out — § 248.30(b) is the only provision excepted from that limit. Everything else in Subpart A sits inside it.

2. THE DEFINITIONS PRODUCE THE SAME RESULT INDEPENDENTLY

Even without § 248.1(b), the defined terms are keyed to personal-purpose individuals (quoted from the same pages):

  • § 248.3(g)(1) "Consumer" — "an individual who obtains or has obtained a financial product or service from you that is to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, or that individual's legal representative."
  • § 248.3(j) "Customer" — "a consumer who has a customer relationship with you."
  • § 248.3(k)(1) "Customer relationship" — "a continuing relationship between a consumer and you under which you provide one or more financial products or services to the consumer that are to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes."
  • § 248.3(f) "Company" — "any corporation, limited liability company, business trust, general or limited partnership, association, or similar organization." The term is defined but is not an object of coverage; it appears in the exclusion and in the third-party/disclosure provisions.
  • § 248.3(t)/(u) "Nonpublic personal information" and "personally identifiable financial information" are both defined by reference to information a consumer provides, or that results from a transaction with a consumer, or that is otherwise obtained about a consumer.

So the coverage chain is: Subpart A obligations → nonpublic personal information → about a consumer → an individual → using the product or service primarily for personal, family, or household purposes. A company can never be a "consumer"; an individual using the product primarily for business, commercial, or agricultural purposes is not a "consumer" and therefore cannot be a "customer" under § 248.3(j)/(k)(1).

3. PROVISION-BY-PROVISION EFFECT (Subpart A)

  • § 248.1 (purpose and scope) — the scope clause itself; excludes company and business-purpose information.
  • § 248.3 (definitions) — consumer/customer/customer relationship all personal-purpose keyed; "company" defined but not covered.
  • § 248.4 (initial notice to consumers) — no obligation to a company or to a business-purpose individual.
  • § 248.5 (annual privacy notice to customers) — obligation runs to "customers" only; no annual notice is owed to a company or to a business-purpose individual. The § 248.5(e) exception (no annual notice where sharing is limited to §§ 248.13–248.15 and policies unchanged) is irrelevant to those populations because they are outside the rule altogether.
  • § 248.6 (content of notices), § 248.7 (opt-out notice and methods), § 248.8 (revised notices), § 248.9 (delivery) — all operate on consumers/customers; no opt-out right arises for company or business-purpose information.
  • §§ 248.13–248.15 (exceptions to notice/opt-out) — exceptions within an already personal-purpose-scoped rule; they do not expand coverage to business information.
  • § 248.30(a) (safeguards) — sits inside the § 248.1(b) scope limit; not a grant of coverage over company information.
  • § 248.30(b) — the single carve-out from § 248.1(b). Its own reach is outside the scope of this question and is not opined on here.
  • Remaining sections of Subpart A contain no independent coverage grant; § 248.1(b) is a subpart-wide limitation ("this subpart applies only to..."), so each of them is confined to personal-purpose consumer information.

4. APPLICATION RULES FOR SCOPING THE ANNUAL NOTICE

  (a) The test is use, not the customer's legal form. § 248.3(g)(1) asks whether the product or service "is to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes." A sole proprietor or business owner who opens an individual brokerage or advisory account for personal purposes is a consumer; a natural person who obtains the product primarily for business, commercial, or agricultural purposes is not.
  (b) Mixed use is resolved by "primarily." Where an account or product serves both personal and business ends, classify by the primary use. Where the record does not establish primary use, document the determination — the rule supplies no presumption.
  (c) Information about a company is excluded even where an individual is the contact, signatory, or principal — unless the information is also nonpublic personal information about that individual in a personal capacity.
  (d) A personal-purpose individual who provides nonpublic personal information in connection with seeking brokerage or investment advisory services is a consumer even if no service is provided and no continuing relationship is established (§ 248.3(g)(2)(i)); but the personal-purpose condition of (g)(1) still governs. A person who provides only name, address, and general areas of investment interest in connection with a prospectus or brochure request is not a consumer (§ 248.3(g)(2)(ii)).
  (e) Practical consequence: the notice population for §§ 248.4–248.9 is the set of personal-purpose consumers/customers. No annual privacy notice, initial notice, opt-out notice, or opt-out right is owed with respect to company information or business-purpose individuals, except to the extent § 248.30(b) independently applies (outside this question).

5. TEMPORAL VALIDITY AS OF 2026-11-21 (STATED LIMITATION)

The text relied on is the eCFR "current" version retrieved 2026-11-23T00:25:28Z — two days after the operative date in the question. The answer should be treated as verified for 2026-11-21 subject to closing that two-day gap:
  (i) Point-in-time text: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-21/title-17.xml?part=248&subpart=A — compare § 248.1(b) word-for-word against the quoted text above.
  (ii) eCFR "Compare Dates" view for 2026-11-21 against current, part 248, subpart A.
  (iii) Federal Register search, agency = Securities and Exchange Commission, CFR part 248, effective dates between 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-23, to confirm no intervening amendment.
  Context supporting stability: the part's source note reads "65 FR 40362, June 29, 2000, unless otherwise noted," with nomenclature changes at 74 FR 40431 (Aug. 11, 2009); the § 248.1(b) scope sentence quoted above is the carried-forward original formulation, and nothing in the grounded text amends it.

6. WHY ASK 1 IS NOT REPORTED AS "NOT STATED"

The harness's proof of absence concerns https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/part-248/section-248.3 only (18,068 characters; fetched 2026-11-23T00:25:28Z, sha256 1a621bf27e88), and only the phrases "business customer," "commercial entity," "business purpose," "business use," "corporate customer," and "entity obtaining financial product for business." That proof does not bear on this ask for three reasons: (i) the answer is not that a page states none — the rule states an express exclusion; (ii) the exclusion is printed in § 248.1(b) on the Subpart A pages, not in the § 248.3 definitions page that was searched; and (iii) the phrases searched are not the words the answer is printed with — the operative words are "business, commercial, or agricultural purposes" and "information about companies," which do appear verbatim in the grounding. Ask 1 is therefore answered as a verdict and appears in neither not_stated nor blocked_on.

7. WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES NOT COVER

Not addressed here, and to be treated as open: the scope of § 248.30(b) itself; 17 CFR Part 248 Subpart B and any other subparts; other regulators' privacy rules (e.g., 12 CFR Part 1016 (Regulation P), 17 CFR Part 160 (CFTC)); GLBA § 503 outside Subpart A; state privacy and data-security law; and contractual confidentiality obligations that may reach business-purpose data even though Subpart A does not. Whether the institution is a "financial institution" under § 248.3 and listed in § 248.1(b) is a separate predicate that this answer assumes rather than decides.

question: Y153
answer:
ANSWER

EUR 20 000. Under Directive (EU) 2015/2366 (PSD2) as originally enacted, a payment institution that provides only the payment service listed in point (6) of Annex I (money remittance) must have capital that 'at no time' falls below EUR 20 000. This is both the initial-capital figure at authorisation (Art. 7(a)) and the hard floor of the ongoing own-funds requirement (Art. 8(1)). It is a floor, not necessarily the whole requirement: the institution must in practice hold the higher of EUR 20 000 and the amount produced by the Article 9 own-funds calculation.

1. LEGAL BASIS (text as enacted)

Article 7 (Initial capital), first paragraph and point (a):

  'Member States shall require payment institutions to hold, at the time of authorisation, initial capital, comprised of one or more of the items referred to in Article 26(1)(a) to (e) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 as follows:
   (a) where the payment institution provides only the payment service as referred to in point (6) of Annex I, its capital shall at no time be less than EUR 20 000;
   (b) where the payment institution provides the payment service as referred to in point (7) of Annex I, its capital shall at no time be less than EUR 50 000;
   (c) where the payment institution provides any of the payment services as referred to in points (1) to (5) of Annex I, its capital shall at no time be less than EUR 125 000.'

Article 8(1) (Own funds):

  'The payment institution's own funds shall not fall below the amount of initial capital as referred to in Article 7 or the amount of own funds as calculated in accordance with Article 9 of this Directive, whichever is the higher.'

Article 9(2)(a) (scaling factor):

  'The scaling factor k to be used in Methods B and C shall be: (a) 0,5 where the payment institution provides only the payment service as referred to in point (6) of Annex I;'

Article 9(3) (supervisory flexibility):

  'The competent authorities may ... require the payment institution to hold an amount of own funds which is up to 20 % higher than the amount which would result from the application of the method chosen in accordance with paragraph 1, or permit the payment institution to hold an amount of own funds which is up to 20 % lower than the amount which would result from the application of the method chosen in accordance with paragraph 1.'

2. WHY 'AT ALL TIMES' IS ANSWERED BY ARTICLE 7(a)

The question's phrase 'at all times' is the directive's own language: Article 7(a) says the capital of a point (6)-only institution 'shall at no time be less than EUR 20 000'. So the figure is not merely a one-off authorisation test; it is a continuous floor. Article 8(1) then fixes the ongoing requirement as max(Art. 7 initial capital, Art. 9 calculated amount). Two consequences:

(a) The EUR 20 000 can never be breached, whatever the Article 9 calculation yields.
(b) The requirement may be higher than EUR 20 000 if the Article 9 calculation exceeds it.

3. THE ARTICLE 9 CALCULATION FOR A POINT (6)-ONLY INSTITUTION

A money-remittance-only institution may use Method A, B or C (Art. 9(1)), subject to the competent authority's assessment; the scaling factor k = 0,5 in Article 9(2)(a) applies to Methods B and C only.

- Method A: own funds at least 10 % of the preceding year's fixed overheads. No k factor applies. If 10 % of fixed overheads is below EUR 20 000, Article 8(1) lifts the requirement back to EUR 20 000.
- Method B: the relevant indicator sliced and multiplied by the Article 9(1)(b) coefficients, the whole multiplied by k = 0,5.
- Method C: 10 % of the preceding year's fixed overheads plus the relevant indicator sliced and multiplied by the Article 9(1)(c) coefficients (2,5 % up to EUR 2,5 m; 8 % from EUR 2,5 m to EUR 5 m; 6 % from EUR 5 m to EUR 25 m; 3 % from EUR 25 m to EUR 50 m; 1,5 % above EUR 50 m), that second component multiplied by k = 0,5.

Worked examples (illustrating that EUR 20 000 is a floor, not a cap). Assume fixed overheads of EUR 150 000 and a relevant indicator of EUR 4 000 000:

- Method A: 10 % x 150 000 = EUR 15 000. Article 8(1): max(20 000; 15 000) = EUR 20 000 -> the floor binds.
- Method B: 4 % x 4 000 000 = EUR 160 000; x k 0,5 = EUR 80 000. Article 8(1): max(20 000; 80 000) = EUR 80 000.
- Method C: (2,5 % x 2 500 000) + (8 % x 1 500 000) = 62 500 + 120 000 = EUR 182 500; x k 0,5 = EUR 91 250; plus 10 % x 150 000 = EUR 15 000 -> EUR 106 250. Article 8(1): max(20 000; 106 250) = EUR 106 250.

In every case the answer to 'what must it maintain at all times' is at least EUR 20 000, and the binding own-funds figure is the larger of EUR 20 000 and the Article 9 result.

4. POINTS THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE EUR 20 000 FLOOR

- The Article 9(3) +/-20 % supervisory adjustment operates on 'the amount which would result from the application of the method chosen in accordance with paragraph 1', i.e. the Article 9 amount. It cannot reduce the Article 7 figure: Article 8(1) sets own funds at the higher of the two, so a permitted 20 % reduction of an Article 9 result of, say, EUR 18 000 would still leave EUR 20 000 as the applicable minimum. The floor is therefore EUR 20 000, not EUR 16 000.
- The k = 0,5 scaling factor for point (6)-only institutions reduces the Article 9 variable component only; it does not touch the Article 7 initial-capital figure.
- The e-money figure of EUR 350 000 (Directive 2009/110/EC) is irrelevant: an e-money institution is a different regime, and the question specifies a payment institution providing only Annex I point (6).
- Article 32 allows Member States to waive authorisation for small money remitters below the turnover thresholds there set; such persons are registered rather than authorised and fall outside the Article 7/8 regime. The question says 'EU payment institution', so the fully authorised regime is assumed; if a national Article 32 waiver were in play, the answer would not be given by Article 7 at all and would need to be re-put.
- The EUR 20 000 figure in Article 7(a) is unchanged from Directive 2007/64/EC Article 6(a) and, on the text available, has not been amended by any subsequent EU act in force; the PSD3/PSR recast proposals are not in force and do not affect the answer under the 2015 directive as enacted.

5. COMPOSITION AND CURRENCY

Initial capital under Article 7 must consist of one or more of the items in Article 26(1)(a) to (e) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CET1 items, with the adjustments there provided). The figure is expressed in euro and is a fixed nominal amount, not index-linked; there is no euro-area conversion issue for a euro-denominated requirement, and Member States that have not adopted the euro apply the equivalent nominal amount under their transposing law. Transposition deadline was 13 January 2018 (Art. 115).

BOTTOM LINE: EUR 20 000, at no time less, per Article 7(a) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366, read with the higher-of rule in Article 8(1).
cautions: The recompute vote did not run, so no figure in this answer was recomputed.
The answer gives 20000 EUR for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: Y154
answer:
Source and version: Regulation (EU) No 648/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on OTC derivatives, central counterparties and trade repositories (EMIR), Article 9, as adopted. The legislation.gov.uk page used is the 'Original (As adopted by EU)' version and states: 'The original version of the legislation as it stood when it was first adopted in the EU. No changes have been applied to the text.' This is therefore the original text, not the later EMIR Refit / amended version.

1. Reporting deadline — Article 9(1)
The operative sentence is:

'Counterparties and CCPs shall ensure that the details of any derivative contract they have concluded and of any modification or termination of the contract are reported to a trade repository registered in accordance with Article 55 or recognised in accordance with Article 77. The details shall be reported no later than the working day following the conclusion, modification or termination of the contract.'

Answer: details of the conclusion, modification or termination must be reported no later than the working day following that conclusion, modification or termination. In shorthand, the deadline is T+1 working day.

The original text uses the term 'working day', not 'business day'. The deadline is not same-day, and it is not a fixed number of calendar days. It applies to counterparties and CCPs, and it is triggered separately by each of the three events: conclusion, modification, and termination. Article 9(1) also permits delegation of reporting and requires reporting without duplication, but neither point changes the deadline.

2. Record-retention period — Article 9(2)
The operative sentence is:

'Counterparties shall keep a record of any derivative contract they have concluded and any modification for at least five years following the termination of the contract.'

Answer: counterparties must keep records of the derivative contract and any modification for at least five years following the termination of the contract. The retention period runs from termination and is a minimum period ('at least five years'), not a maximum or a fixed period ending earlier. The obligation is placed on 'Counterparties' in Article 9(2); Article 9(1)'s reporting obligation is placed on 'Counterparties and CCPs'.

Resulting values:
- Ask 1: 1 working day following the conclusion, modification or termination (statutory wording: 'no later than the working day following').
- Ask 2: 5 years following termination (statutory wording: 'at least five years following the termination of the contract').

No ask is listed in not_stated: the adopted Article 9 page does not state that the answer is absent; it states the deadline using 'working day following'. The proof of absence for ask 1 rules out paraphrases using 'business day' and similar wording, but it does not rule out the actual statutory phrase 'working day following', which is present in the quoted Article 9(1) text.

question: Y155
answer:
REGULATORY POSITION — 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2): 7-calendar-day clock for unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reactions

1. ANSWER

A sponsor must notify FDA of any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction as soon as possible, and in no case later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information.

Controlling value: 7 calendar days, measured from initial receipt (not from the sponsor's later determination that the event is reportable).
Citation: 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2).

2. OPERATIVE TEXT (verbatim, as supplied)

"(2) Unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction reports. The sponsor must also notify FDA of any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction as soon as possible but in no case later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information."
— 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2); confirmed identical in all four supplied fetches of section 312.32 (eCFR HTML, eCFR part 312, govinfo CFR 2025 PDF, alternate eCFR URL).

Note on the grounding's proof of absence: the harness searched only for the paraphrases "within 7 days", "no later than 7 days", "7 days", "seven days", "within seven calendar days", and "within 7 calendar days". The regulation uses none of those forms; it says "in no case later than 7 calendar days". Because the actual phrasing was not among the searched strings, the negative result is an artifact of the search vocabulary and does not establish that the page is silent. The answer is stated on the page, verbatim, and is therefore reported as a value rather than listed as not stated.

3. RULE DECOMPOSITION

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Trigger | An adverse event that is (a) unexpected, (b) fatal or life-threatening, and (c) a suspected adverse reaction (i.e., there is evidence to suggest a causal relationship between the drug and the event — 312.32(c)(1)(i)). |
| Standard | "As soon as possible" — an independent, potentially earlier obligation. The 7 days is an outer limit, not a target. |
| Clock start | The sponsor's initial receipt of the information. Not the date of case adjudication, not the date of the causality assessment, not the date of the safety review committee meeting. |
| Clock length | 7 calendar days. Calendar days, not working days. The text provides no weekend or Federal-holiday extension and no provision for FDA to grant one. |
| Recipient | FDA. (Contrast 312.32(c)(1), which requires the IND safety report to go to FDA and all participating investigators; (c)(2) by its terms names FDA.) |
| Vehicle | Notification to FDA; 312.32(c)(1) establishes the IND safety report as the reporting vehicle for (c)(1)(i)-(iv), and (c)(3) permits FDA to require a different format or frequency, or the sponsor to adopt one if agreed in advance by the responsible FDA review division director. |
| Follow-up | 312.32(d)(2): relevant follow-up information must be submitted as soon as it is available and identified as a "Followup IND Safety Report." 312.32(d)(1): the sponsor must promptly investigate all safety information it receives. |

4. CLOCK ARITHMETIC — HOW TO COUNT THE 7 DAYS

Convention: Day 0 = the calendar date on which any personnel or agent of the sponsor first receives information meeting the trigger. Day 0 is not counted. The deadline is Day 0 + 7 calendar days, at the end of that day. Weekends and Federal holidays are counted.

Worked examples (all satisfy the 7-calendar-day bound; none exceeds it):

| Initial receipt (Day 0) | Day 1 | Deadline (Day 7) |
|---|---|---|
| Mon 2 Mar 2026 | Tue 3 Mar | Mon 9 Mar 2026 |
| Tue 3 Mar 2026 | Wed 4 Mar | Tue 10 Mar 2026 |
| Fri 6 Mar 2026 | Sat 7 Mar | Fri 13 Mar 2026 |
| Thu 24 Dec 2026 | Fri 25 Dec | Thu 31 Dec 2026 |
| Sun 27 Dec 2026 | Mon 28 Dec | Sun 3 Jan 2027 |

(Verify one row by hand: 3 Mar + 7 = 10 Mar. Correct.)

Because the count is in calendar days, a receipt on a Friday does not buy extra time; the internal submission must be completed by the following Friday at the latest. Where the 7th day falls on a weekend or holiday, the regulatory outer limit does not move — plan internal release so that filing does not depend on same-day staffing.

5. RELATIONSHIP TO THE OTHER PART 312 DEADLINES (do not conflate)

| Deadline | Length | Clock starts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction | 7 calendar days | Sponsor's initial receipt of the information | 312.32(c)(2) |
| Other serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction (incl. findings from other studies, animal studies, epidemiological studies, pooled analyses) | 15 calendar days | Sponsor's determination that the information qualifies for reporting | 312.32(c)(1) |
| Event not initially judged reportable but later found reportable on investigation | 15 calendar days | The determination is made | 312.32(d)(3) |
| Additional data or information requested by FDA | 15 calendar days | Receipt of FDA's request | 312.32(c)(1) (final sentence) |
| Relevant follow-up to an IND safety report | As soon as available | Availability | 312.32(d)(2) |
| Discontinuance for unreasonable and significant risk | 5 working days | The determination to discontinue | 312.56(d) |

The 7-day figure is the shortest deadline in Part 312 and is the one that governs here. A case that is initially reported on the 7-day clock still requires the follow-up submission under (d)(2), and still appears in the annual report summary of IND safety reports under 312.33.

6. OPERATING PROCEDURE (sponsor-side implementation)

Step 1 — Day 0 stamping. On first receipt by any sponsor personnel or agent (clinical operations, pharmacovigilance intake, medical monitor, contractor, licensee), record: date and time of receipt, source document, receiver identity, and the verbatim event description. This timestamp is the clock start and the defensible record of it. Do not re-set Day 0 on internal transmission.

Step 2 — Triage (internal target: within 24 hours of Day 0; internal practice, not a regulatory figure). Determine: unexpected (not listed at the observed specificity/severity in the investigator brochure or, for a marketed drug, the labeling)? fatal or life-threatening? evidence to suggest a causal relationship? If yes to all three, the case is on the 7-day clock.

Step 3 — Escalation. Notify the responsible medical monitor and the head of pharmacovigilance the same business day. Open the 7-day case record with the computed deadline printed on it (Day 0 + 7).

Step 4 — Internal hard stop at Day 5. Complete the narrative, the causality statement, the expectedness assessment against the reference safety information, and the cross-reference to prior similar reports. Submit to FDA no later than Day 5 to preserve two days of contingency against the Day 7 outer limit.

Step 5 — Submission. Notify FDA by the means the IND and any FDA-agreed format provide. Identify the submission as an IND safety report; identify all previously submitted IND safety reports concerning a similar suspected adverse reaction and analyze the significance of the reaction in light of them (312.32(c)(1)).

Step 6 — Follow-up. Continue the investigation (312.32(d)(1)); submit relevant follow-up as soon as available, labeled "Followup IND Safety Report" (312.32(d)(2)). If the investigation reclassifies a previously non-reportable event as reportable, report within 15 calendar days of that determination (312.32(d)(3)).

Step 7 — Recordkeeping. Retain the Day 0 timestamp, the triage decision, the expectedness and causality assessments, the submission transmittal, and the follow-up correspondence for the period required by 312.57(c) (2 years after marketing application approval, or 2 years after shipment and delivery for investigational use is discontinued and FDA is notified).

Step 8 — Consequence awareness. Failure to promptly investigate and inform FDA and all investigators of serious and unexpected adverse experiences in accordance with 312.32 is a ground for clinical hold under 312.42(b)(1)(x) as reflected in the supplied part 312 text.

7. LIMITS OF THE SUPPLIED TEXT — flagged, not invented

The following are commonly asked alongside this question but are not resolved by the supplied passages, and I do not assert them as regulatory requirements here:

- Notification channel. The supplied text of 312.32(c)(2) names no channel (telephone, fax, electronic). 312.32(c)(3) allows FDA to require a different format or frequency, and the sponsor to adopt one if agreed in advance by the responsible review division director. Any channel requirement must be confirmed against the IND and FDA's current guidance, not against the quoted text.
- Definitional scope of "initial receipt" as applied to information held by a foreign affiliate, licensee, or contractor. The quoted text does not address it. Confirm against 312.32(a) definitions and current FDA guidance before relying on any position.
- Weekend/holiday relief. The quoted text grants none. Do not plan on one.

8. BOTTOM LINE

Seven calendar days from the sponsor's initial receipt of the information — 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2) — with a concurrent obligation to notify as soon as possible, which in practice will often be earlier than day 7.

question: Y156
answer:
CONCLUSION

Under 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, as in force on 2026-11-21, a person required to register its establishment under § 807.20 who proposes to begin the introduction, or delivery for introduction, into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device requiring premarket notification must submit the premarket notification submission (510(k)) to FDA AT LEAST 90 DAYS BEFORE that proposed introduction or delivery for introduction.

Answer: 90 days (a minimum lead time; calendar days).

1. OPERATIVE TEXT

21 CFR § 807.81(a) (eCFR, Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H, Part 807, Subpart E), verbatim:

"(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:
(1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, (i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or (ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.
(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.
(3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. ..."

Source citation line as printed: "[42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 72 FR 73601, Dec. 28, 2007; 89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024]" — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-807/subpart-E/section-807.81 (retrieved 2026-11-23).

2. HOW THE ELEMENTS OF THE QUESTION MAP ONTO THE TEXT

- 'Person required to register its establishment under § 807.20' — the addressee of § 807.81(a); the duty attaches to that registrant, not to the device owner generally.
- 'Introduce or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce' — the regulation uses the compound phrase 'introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution'; the 90-day clock runs from the earlier of the two events the registrant 'proposes to begin.' There is no separate or longer lead time for 'delivery for introduction' as distinct from 'introduction'; both are measured against the same 90-day minimum.
- 'Device that requires premarket notification' — i.e., a device meeting § 807.81(a)(1), (a)(2), or (a)(3) and not within the § 807.81(b) exclusions or the § 807.85 exemptions. Because the question stipulates the device requires notification, the 90-day figure applies without further classification analysis.
- 'How long before' — 90 days, minimum. It is a floor, not a fixed or maximum interval: submitting earlier is permitted and common (a 510(k) may be submitted many months before launch).

3. VERSION / CURRENCY VERIFICATION (as of 2026-11-21)

- The eCFR text retrieved 2026-11-23 carries a last amendment of 89 FR 18792 (Mar. 15, 2024), which added the predetermined change control plan (PCCP) carve-out at § 807.81(b)(1)(ii). That amendment changed what is exempt from notification; it did not alter the 'at least 90 days' lead time in paragraph (a).
- No Federal Register rulemaking in the record amends § 807.81 between Mar. 15, 2024 and 2026-11-21. The 2026 document in the record (91 FR 13310 / Docket No. FDA-2026-N-1849, published 2026-07-22) is an OMB Paperwork Reduction Act notice concerning the information collection burden of Part 807 Subpart E; it is not a rule and does not change the timing requirement. It in fact describes Subpart E as the continuing 'PREMARKET NOTIFICATION PROCEDURES' collection, confirming the subpart remains in force.
- Therefore the 90-day rule is the rule in force on 2026-11-21.

4. QUALIFICATIONS A REGULATORY REVIEWER SHOULD CARRY FORWARD

(a) Minimum submission lead time is not a marketing authorization. Submitting 90 days before the intended launch date satisfies § 807.81(a)'s timing obligation, but the device may not be introduced into commercial distribution until FDA issues a determination of substantial equivalence (or the device is otherwise legally marketed). The 90 days is a floor on when the submission must be made, not a guaranteed clearance interval; launch dates should be planned around FDA's actual review, not the 90-day minimum.

(b) Exceptions in § 807.81(b): no premarket notification is required where a PMA under section 515 or a reclassification petition under section 513(f)(2) is pending before FDA, or where a PCCP cleared under section 515C covers the change and the change is consistent with the PCCP. Where an exception applies, the 90-day clock does not run because no submission is due.

(c) Exemptions: § 807.85 (custom devices) and class I/II exemptions under section 510(l) remove the notification obligation, and with it the 90-day clock.

(d) Radiation-emitting products: § 807.81(c) adds Part 1002 reporting obligations but does not change the 90-day lead time.

(e) The lead time runs to the proposed date of beginning introduction or delivery for introduction; a slip in the launch date does not create a new filing obligation, but a launch moved earlier than 90 days after submission leaves the submission late relative to § 807.81(a).

5. SCOPING NOTE ON THE PROOF OF ABSENCE

The record contains a full-text search of § 807.90 (Format of a premarket notification submission; 1,754 characters) showing that '90 days,' 'ninety days,' '90-day period,' and similar phrasings do not appear there. That is expected and immaterial: § 807.90 governs addressing and format (where to send the submission, single electronic version, separate submission per product, cover-letter designation), not timing. The timing rule lives in § 807.81(a), which was retrieved in full and states 'at least 90 days' expressly. The absence of the phrase on the § 807.90 page is therefore not an absence of the answer, and the ask is answered, not reported as unstated.

6. ONE-LINE CITABLE ANSWER

'At least 90 days before the proposed introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution.' — 21 CFR § 807.81(a) (as amended through 89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024; text in force 2026-11-21).

question: Y157
answer:
## ICH E6(R2) — IRB/IEC composition: answers

### Bottom line

| Ask | Answer | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Recommended minimum total membership | **5 members** ("At least five members") | ICH E6(R2) §3.2.1(a) |
| 2. Two membership characteristics to be included | **(b) at least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area; (c) at least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site** | ICH E6(R2) §3.2.1(b) and (c) |

### Controlling text (verbatim, ICH E6(R2) §3.2.1)

> **3.2 Composition, Functions and Operations**
> **3.2.1** The IRB/IEC should consist of a reasonable number of members, who collectively have the qualifications and experience to review and evaluate the science, medical aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial. It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should include:
> (a) At least five members.
> (b) At least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area.
> (c) At least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site.
> Only those IRB/IEC members who are independent of the investigator and the sponsor of the trial should vote/provide opinion on a trial-related matter.
> A list of IRB/IEC members and their qualifications should be maintained.

This wording is identical across the three independently fetched copies of E6(R2) in the source set (US/FDA copy uses "favorable", the TGA and EMA copies "favourable"; the composition list itself is word-for-word the same in all three).

### Ask 1 — minimum total membership: 5

- The number is **five**, and it is a **floor, not a target**: the same subsection opens by requiring "a reasonable number of members, who collectively have the qualifications and experience to review and evaluate the science, medical aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial." A five-person committee that cannot collectively cover science + medical + ethics does not satisfy §3.2.1 even though it satisfies (a).
- The obligation is phrased as "It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should include" — in E6(R2) drafting convention "should" denotes a recommendation/expectation rather than an absolute legal mandate; the binding force comes from the implementing jurisdiction (see 'Limits' below). For any practical purpose (SOP drafting, inspection readiness), treat 5 as the minimum acceptable composition.
- E6(R2) does **not** prescribe a numeric quorum. §3.2.3 leaves quorum to the IRB/IEC's own written operating procedures ("at least a quorum, as stipulated in its written operating procedures"). Do not state a quorum number as an E6(R2) requirement.
- Nonmembers with expertise in special areas may be invited to assist (§3.2.6) but are **not members** and do not count toward the five.

### Ask 2 — the two membership characteristics

**(b) At least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area.**
- The test is the member's *primary area of interest*, not their degree. A physician whose main interest is clinical care is scientific; a lawyer, ethicist, clergyperson, patient advocate, or layperson whose principal interest is outside science satisfies (b).
- The guideline deliberately says "nonscientific", not "non-medical" and not "lay": a member from another scientific discipline (e.g., a statistician or a bench scientist from a different field) does **not** automatically satisfy (b).

**(c) At least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site.**
- Independence here is independence from the **institution / trial site**, i.e., not employed by, not otherwise affiliated with, and not in a dependent relationship with the institution or site conducting the trial.
- This is a *different* test from the voting rule in the closing paragraph of §3.2.1 ("independent of the investigator and the sponsor"). Independence from the site is a composition requirement; independence from investigator and sponsor is a voting-eligibility requirement. Both must be satisfied, and they are assessed member by member.

**Do (b) and (c) have to be different people?** E6(R2) does not say so expressly; each is a separate sub-requirement, and a single person could in principle hold both attributes. In practice, constitute them as **two separate seats** — the widely applied reading (and the structure used in the regional overlays, e.g. 45 CFR 46.107(c)–(d), which separates the non-affiliated member from the member whose primary concerns are nonscientific) treats them as distinct, and separate seats are far easier to defend at inspection.

### Related composition/operations rules that are NOT the answer to either ask

Stated here so they are not confused with (a)–(c):
- §3.2.1 — only members independent of the investigator and sponsor vote/opine on a trial-related matter.
- §3.2.1 — a list of members and their qualifications must be maintained.
- §3.2.3 — decisions at announced meetings with at least a quorum as defined in written procedures (no number given).
- §3.2.4 — only members who participate in review and discussion vote/opine/advise.
- §3.2.6 — nonmembers with special expertise may be invited; they are not members.
- §3.3.1 — written procedures must cover determining composition (names and qualifications) and the authority under which the committee is established.
- §3.4 — records (including membership lists and lists of occupations/affiliations) retained at least 3 years after trial completion.

### Why ask 2 is answered here and is NOT recorded as 'not stated'

The harness's proof of absence searched the FDA, TGA and EMA copies for the strings "scientific expertise", "non‑scientific expertise", "lay member", "community member" and "ethics expertise", and found none. That result is correct but does not bear on ask 2, for three reasons:
1. **Wrong strings.** E6(R2) does not use any of those phrases. The operative wording is "primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area" and "independent of the institution/trial site".
2. **Those exact operative strings are present** in all three fetched pages and are quoted verbatim in the grounding (the TGA fetch returns them as standalone quotes: "At least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area." / "At least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site.").
3. **Mechanical mismatch.** The searched term "non‑scientific expertise" carries a non-ASCII hyphen and the word "expertise"; it could not match the guideline's "nonscientific" in any case.

So the page does not state "none"; it states the answer. Recording ask 2 in `not_stated` would misreport the source, so `not_stated` is empty. If a future search is run, the strings to use are: "nonscientific", "independent of the institution", "at least five members".

REGULATORY DETERMINATION — HUD PREVALENCE CEILING UNDER 21 CFR PART 814 (IN FORCE 2026-11-21)

1. ANSWER

The prevalence ceiling the legacy HDE checklist must use is 8,000 individuals in the United States per year. The checklist's 4,000 figure is superseded and must be corrected.

Controlling citation: 21 CFR 814.3(n) (definition of "HUD").

Secondary/confirming citations: 21 CFR 814.100(b); 21 CFR 814.102(a)(5); 21 CFR 814.102(b)(3)(i)-(ii).

2. CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, eCFR current, fetched 2026-11-23T00:34:47Z, sha256 a92b8b1d4ba3)

"Sec. 814.3 Definitions.
For the purposes of this part:
...
(m) HDE means a premarket approval application submitted pursuant to this subpart seeking a humanitarian device exemption from the effectiveness requirements of sections 514 and 515 of the act as authorized by section 520(m)(2) of the act.
(n) HUD (humanitarian use device) means a medical device intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of a disease or condition that affects or is manifested in not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year."

Note the structural point the checklist must respect: the prevalence ceiling lives in the definition of "HUD" at 814.3(n), not in the definition of "HDE" at 814.3(m). 814.3(m) defines the HDE as the application type and contains no prevalence number. The checklist should cite 814.3(n).

3. CORROBORATION ACROSS SUBPART H (all read 8,000)

- 21 CFR 814.100(b): "...to encourage the discovery and use of devices intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of diseases or conditions that affect or are manifested in not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year."
- 21 CFR 814.102(a)(5): "...to demonstrate that the device is designed to treat or diagnose a disease or condition that affects or is manifested in not more than 8,000 people in the United States per year. If the device is for diagnostic purposes, the documentation must demonstrate that not more than 8,000 patients per year would be subjected to diagnosis by the device in the United States."
- 21 CFR 814.102(b)(3)(i): "...affects or is manifested in not more than 8,000 people in the United States per year"; (ii): "...for a diagnostic device, more than 8,000 patients in the United States would be subjected to diagnosis using the device per year".

4. VERSION / CURRENCY VERIFICATION (satisfies the 'as in force on 2026-11-21' constraint)

Evidence set, all consistent at 8,000:
(a) eCFR "current" Part 814 and Sec. 814.3 pages, fetched 2026-11-23T00:34:47Z (sha256 7c4288803759 and a92b8b1d4ba3) — 8,000.
(b) GovInfo CFR-2022 title 21 vol 8, Part 814 XML (sha256 f770dfc8d8d7) — 8,000.
(c) GovInfo CFR-2021 title 21 vol 8, Part 814 PDF (sha256 91271e8b2d80) — 8,000.

  GET https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-21/title-21.xml?part=814&section=814.3

4,000 was the original statutory/regulatory ceiling for the humanitarian use device prevalence standard. It was raised to 8,000 by the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255, enacted 2016-12-13), with FDA's conforming rulemaking published at 82 FR 26349 (June 7, 2017). The 2017 conforming amendment is directly evidenced in the current eCFR text: Sec. 814.102 carries the source note "[61 FR 33244, June 26, 1996, as amended at 82 FR 26349, June 7, 2017]". The Cures Act attribution of the 4,000-to-8,000 change is standard regulatory history and should be cited to the statute (Pub. L. 114-255, Sec. 3052) and 82 FR 26349 in any external-facing document; verify the section number of the public law against the enrolled bill before it appears in a submission.

Consequence for legacy items: a checklist written before 2017 is not describing a different pathway — it is quoting a ceiling that no longer exists. Existing HUD designations granted under the former 4,000 standard are not automatically invalidated by the increase; 814.102(c) supplies the exclusive revocation grounds (untrue statement of material fact or omitted material information; or the device is not eligible for HUD designation based on available evidence). # Answer — CDC 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis'

## 1. Source identified and version pinned

- **Page (URL):** https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/ — breadcrumb 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis', section 'For Health Care Providers'.
- **Content date shown on the page:** Apr. 17, 2025.

The retrieved text is therefore the version in force on 2026-11-21 unless an unrecorded revision occurred inside that 2-day window. Residual risk: low; closable by diffing against a Wayback snapshot dated on or before 2026-11-21. This is a flagged caveat, not a blocker — the substantive sentences below are stable across the page and its two companion CDC TST sources.

## 2. Ask 1 — When must the TST reaction be examined

**Direct quote from the target page (sha256 `9095c1db7f3e`):**

> "After 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker."

> "The health care worker measures the induration (firm swelling) where the tuberculin was injected to determine if the reaction to the test is positive or negative."

**Answer: the reaction is examined 48–72 hours after the tuberculin is injected** — i.e., 48–72 hours after placement/administration of the Mantoux TST. The clock runs from placement, not from the clinic visit or from the reading appointment.

**Operational corollaries from CDC's own TST material (same 48–72 window, no conflict):**
- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html (content date Jan. 31, 2025; sha256 `4aa43e3065d3`): "The skin test reaction should be read between 48 and 72 hours after administration by a health care worker trained to read TB skin results."
- Same page, 72-hour outer bound enforced: "A patient who does not return within 72 hours will need to be rescheduled for another skin test."
- CDC TST factsheet PDF (sha256 `8e42decc7a4c`): "The skin test reaction should be read between 48 and 72 hours after administration by a health care worker trained to read TST results. A patient who does not return within 72 hours will need to be rescheduled for another skin test."
- Measurement rule at reading: record millimeters of **induration** (firm swelling), not erythema; measure across the forearm, perpendicular to its long axis.
- Do not let the reading window delay diagnosis: "If a patient has symptoms of TB disease, health care providers should not wait for TB skin test results before starting other diagnostic tests." (TST subpage)

## 3. Ask 2 — Who must examine it

**Direct quotes from the target page:**

> "After 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker."

> "TB skin results should only be read by a trained health care professional. Consult with your state and local public health authorities to determine who is authorized to place and read TB skin tests in your state."

**Companion page, same requirement, fuller wording** (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html, sha256 `4aa43e3065d3`):

> "The TB skin test should be placed (administered) and read by a designated, trained health care provider. Consult with your state and local public health authorities to determine who is authorized to place and read TB skin tests in your state."

> "Training is essential for health care providers to gain proficiency in the administration and interpretation of the TB skin test."

**Answer: the reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker / trained health care professional — a designated, trained health care provider.** The CDC-level qualification is *training and designation in TST placement and reading*; training is stated to be essential for proficiency.

**Boundary the page itself sets (do not overstate):** the page does **not** name a specific license, credential, or job class (e.g., RN, LVN, MD, medical assistant) as the reader. It explicitly delegates that to **state and local public health authorities** ("determine who is authorized to place and read TB skin tests in your state"). Any statement that CDC requires a particular license would be an addition to this source.

## 4. Why ask 1 is NOT reported as 'page states none'

The harness recorded a proof of absence for ask 1 on this page against five phrase variants: "48–72 hours after placement", "within 48–72 hours", "2–3 days after placement", "72 hours post‑placement", "at 48–72 hours" — none found. That result is a **string-match artifact, not an absence of content**: the page's actual sentence is "**After** 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined...", which begins with "After" followed by a comma and therefore matches none of the five patterns. The substantive answer appears verbatim in the full text of the same page (sha256 `9095c1db7f3e`) and is reproduced in the grounding's own quoted passages.

Therefore ask 1 is answered from the page and is **not** listed in `not_stated`. A reviewer can confirm in one step: search the page text for the string `After 48–72 hours`.

## 5. Consolidated answer as delivered to a clinician

1. **Timing:** read the Mantoux TST reaction **48–72 hours after placement**. Outside 72 hours, the reading is not valid — the patient must be rescheduled for a new TST. If TB disease is suspected, do not hold other diagnostics for the skin test result.
2. **Reader:** a **trained/designated health care worker (health care professional/provider)** trained to read TB skin results. Confirm with your state or local public health authority which licensed personnel in your jurisdiction are authorized to place and read TSTs.
3. **At reading:** measure induration in millimeters (not erythema), across the forearm perpendicular to its long axis; interpret against the patient's risk factors.

## Answer

**45 days.** Under 21 CFR 814.42(a), FDA must notify a PMA applicant whether the application has been filed within **45 days after FDA receives the PMA**. The count is in calendar days, not business days (basis below).

## Governing text (verbatim)

21 CFR 814.42 — Filing a PMA:

> "(a) The filing of an application means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the application is sufficiently complete to permit a substantive review. **Within 45 days after a PMA is received by FDA, the agency will notify the applicant whether the application has been filed.**
>
> (b) If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (e) of this section for refusing to file the PMA applies, the agency will file the PMA and will notify the applicant in writing of the filing. The notice will include the PMA reference number and the date FDA filed the PMA. The date of filing is the date that a PMA accepted for filing was received by the agency. The 180-day period for review of a PMA starts on the date of filing.
>
> (c) If FDA refuses to file a PMA, the agency will notify the applicant of the reasons for the refusal. This notice will identify the deficiencies in the application that prevent filing and will include the PMA reference number."

Source note carried with the section: "[51 FR 26364, July 22, 1986, as amended at 63 FR 5254, Feb. 2, 1998; 73 FR 49942, Aug. 25, 2008; 85 FR 18442, Apr. 2, 2020]" (eCFR); the GovInfo CFR 2025 XML prints the same section with "...as amended at 87 FR 2045, Jan. 13, 2022". The two source notes differ in editorial detail; **the operative sentence is character-for-character identical in both**, and identical again on FDA's PMA Review Process page and in the eCFR subchapter-level page.

## Calendar days, not business days

The regulation says "days" unqualified in § 814.42(a). The same section demonstrates the drafters' convention when business days are meant:

> § 814.42(d)(2): "Request in writing within **10 working days** of the date of receipt of the notice refusing to file the PMA, an informal conference ... FDA will hold the informal conference within **10 working days** of its receipt of the request and will render its decision on filing within **5 working days** after the informal conference."

Where Part 814 intends working days it says "working days." The 45-day filing notice carries no such qualifier, so it is 45 calendar days. (The 180-day, 7-day, 30-day and 75-day periods quoted elsewhere in Part 814 are likewise unqualified "days" and are read as calendar days on the same basis.)

**Counting convention:** the clock runs from the date FDA receives the PMA; the day of receipt is the reference point and day 1 is the next day. Worked example: a PMA received Monday 2 November 2026 must draw its filing notice by **Thursday 17 December 2026** (28 days to 30 November, plus 17 days in December). An inclusive count from the receipt date would yield 16 December; practitioners should diarize the earlier of the two.

## What this figure is NOT (guarding against conflation)

| Item | Period | Provision |
|---|---|---|
| **PMA filing notification (the answer)** | **45 days after receipt** | **21 CFR 814.42(a)** |
| PMA substantive review clock | 180 days from date of filing | 21 CFR 814.42(b) |
| HDE filing notification | 30 days from receipt | 21 CFR 814.112(a) |
| HDE decision after accepted filing | 75 days | 21 CFR 814.114 |
| OPEQ Director decision on reconsideration of a refusal-to-file | 60 days from receipt of request | FDA PMA Review Process page |
| Applicant request to meet on review status | within 100 days of filing | FDA PMA Review Process page |
| Applicant response to amendment/approvable/not-approvable letter (else deemed withdrawn) | 180 days | 21 CFR 814.44(g) |

None of these is 45 days; only § 814.42(a) is. Note also that the 45-day period governs the **filing/acceptance threshold determination only** — it is not the approval decision and it does not stop the separate 180-day review clock, which begins on the date of filing.

## Point-in-time verification (as in force on 2026-11-21)

- Text checked: 2026-11-23T00:38:17Z (eCFR "current" Part 814, sha256 7c4288803759; § 814.42 page, sha256 1c98fcec130a; eCFR subchapter-C Part 814, sha256 7c4288803759; GovInfo CFR-2025-title21-vol8 Part 814 PDF, sha256 bb5f25146fd9; GovInfo Subpart C XML, sha256 9982d07e7ca4; FDA PMA Review Process page, sha256 3b780da1bd0f).
- The latest amendment recorded against § 814.42 in any source is **87 FR 2045, January 13, 2022**. Nothing in the grounding evidences an amendment to § 814.42(a) taking effect between that date and 2026-11-21, and the CFR-2025 bound volume prints the 45-day text unchanged.
- Residual gap, stated plainly: the fetch is two days **after** the target date. The eCFR "current" text at 2026-11-23 and the CFR-2025 volume are therefore being used as the best available evidence of the text on 2026-11-21, supported by the amendment history ending in 2022. To close the gap definitively, run the eCFR point-in-time query — `https://www.ecfr.gov/on/2026-11-21/title-21/section-814.42` — and confirm the operative sentence still reads "Within 45 days" and that the authority note lists no amendment dated between 2022-01-13 and 2026-11-21.

## On the harness's proof of absence

The harness searched the full text of all six pages and found none of "15 days", "fifteen days", "15-day period", "15 days after receipt", "15 days after FDA receives a PMA". That result is correctly read as **excluding a 15-day figure** from Part 814 — it is not a statement that the pages are silent on the question. The same full texts contain the 45-day sentence, quoted above and repeated verbatim on the eCFR Part 814 page, the § 814.42 page, the GovInfo PDF, the GovInfo Subpart C XML, the eCFR subchapter page, and FDA's PMA Review Process page. Ask 1 is therefore answered, not not-stated, and it is not blocked.

## Assumptions and scope

1. Scope is an **original PMA**. PMA supplements, HDEs, 510(k)s and IDEs have their own timelines and are out of scope; the 30-day HDE figure in the table is a contrast only and must never be substituted for the PMA figure.
2. "Days" = calendar days, per the working-days contrast in § 814.42(d)(2).
3. "Receives" means the date FDA receives the submission; where FDA refuses to file and the applicant resubmits, § 814.42(d)(1) resets the reference date to the date FDA receives the resubmission, and where a refusal-to-file is reversed after an informal conference, the date of filing becomes the date of the decision to accept (§ 814.42(d)(2)). The 45-day notification duty in § 814.42(a) applies to the original receipt.
4. A statement of the answer should be re-verified against eCFR before being relied on for any date later than 2026-11-23, since the figure is asserted as of a point in time.

REGULATORY DETERMINATION — 21 CFR Part 860 (Subpart D), version in force 2026-11-21

QUESTION: FDA receives a De Novo request that is accepted without any additional-information submission. What are the outside time limits (a) for FDA's acceptance notification and (b) for FDA's review and order granting or declining the request?

ANSWER
(a) Acceptance notification: 15 days after FDA receives the De Novo request.
(b) Review and granting/declining order: 120 days after FDA receives the De Novo request.
Both periods run from the same event — FDA's receipt of the request — so they run concurrently. The outside limit for the entire matter, measured from receipt, is 120 days. It is NOT 135 days; the 120-day clock does not start on the acceptance date.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT

1.1 Acceptance notification — 21 CFR 860.230(a):
"The acceptance of a De Novo request means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the De Novo request contains the information necessary to permit a substantive review. Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted."

1.2 Deemed acceptance if the acceptance review is not completed — 21 CFR 860.230(b):
"If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (c)(1) of this section for refusing to accept the De Novo request apply or FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA accepted the De Novo request. The date of acceptance is the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA."
Two operative consequences: (i) 15 days is both the notification deadline and the outer bound of the acceptance review itself — if FDA does not finish within 15 days, acceptance is automatic and the notification obligation continues; (ii) the date of acceptance is back-dated to the date of receipt, which is why the 120-day clock and the 15-day clock share a single start date.

1.3 Review and order — 21 CFR 860.240(a):
"FDA will begin substantive review of a De Novo request after the De Novo request is accepted under § 860.230. Within 120 days after receipt of a De Novo request or receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under § 860.230, FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting the De Novo request under § 860.260(a) or an order declining the De Novo request under 860.260(b)."
The 120-day clock has two possible triggers: receipt of the request, or receipt of additional information that results in acceptance. Because the stipulated facts exclude any additional-information submission (no refusal to accept, no supplemental submission), the operative trigger is receipt of the request itself.

2. VERSION IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21
Identical text appears in (i) the eCFR "current" page for 21 CFR 860.230 (fetched 2026-11-23T00:40:24Z, sha256 4b51e14960fd), (ii) the eCFR "current" page for 21 CFR Part 860 carrying § 860.240(a) (sha256 fffe7e6cc6c5), (iii) the eCFR Subpart D page (sha256 836c1be841b1), (iv) the GovInfo XML of CFR-2025-title21-vol8 § 860.230 (sha256 7fe7db912fc0), and (v) the GovInfo PDF of CFR-2025-title21-vol8 Part 860 Subpart D (sha256 917b0d666508). The GovInfo 2025 print edition carries an effective date of 2025-04-01 and already contains both the 15-day and 120-day periods. The only editorial note on Part 860 in the fetched text is a nomenclature note (73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008; 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021), neither of which touches these periods. No amendment affecting § 860.230(a) or § 860.240(a) appears between the 2025-04-01 edition and the current eCFR snapshot, so the figures 15 and 120 govern on 2026-11-21.

3. DAY-COUNTING AND TRIGGER
- Trigger for both periods: the date FDA receives the De Novo request. § 860.230(b) fixes the acceptance date as the date of receipt; § 860.240(a) runs from "receipt."
- Unit: the regulation says "days" with no business-day qualifier. Treat as calendar days. Caveat: Part 860 does not itself state a counting convention; the calendar-day reading is the standard FDA convention for these periods and is an interpretation, not quoted text.
- Concurrency: day 15 (notification) and day 120 (order) are counted from the same day. Worked example — request received 2026-11-21: notification due no later than 2026-12-06; order due no later than 2027-03-21 (using the convention that the receipt date is day 0). If a requester instead counted 120 days from the acceptance date, it would wrongly produce a day-135 outside limit.

4. WHAT DOES NOT AFFECT THE ANSWER
- Submission method (electronic vs. paper): neither § 860.230 nor § 860.240 conditions the 15-day or 120-day period on submission format. The only format-linked rule is substantive (refusal to accept for failure to follow § 860.210 formatting), which is a ground for refusal, not a different clock.
- MDUFA performance goals: commitments in FDA's performance-goals letters are not regulatory outside limits. The outside limits are the two periods codified in Part 860 above.
- Additional-information tolling: the stipulated facts exclude it. For completeness, on the face of the text the only restart of the 120-day period is "additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted" (i.e., after a refusal to accept under § 860.230(c)). A mid-review request for additional information under § 860.240(b)(1) does not, by the terms of § 860.240(a), restart or extend the 120 days.
- The 30-day figure: the only 30-day period in Subpart D near this subject matter is in § 860.260(a)(2), which attaches to a step following issuance of an order granting a De Novo request ("If FDA grants a De Novo request, within 30 days after the issuance of an order granting the De Novo request..."). It is not an acceptance-notification deadline and must not be substituted for the 15-day period. This is the reconciliation of the harness's proof of absence: the search confirms § 860.230 contains no "30 days" string; § 860.230 does contain the affirmative 15-day text quoted at 1.1. The page therefore states an answer rather than stating none, and ask 1 is not listed as not stated.

5. RELATED DEADLINES IN THE SAME SUBPART (for scoping, not part of the answer)
- Withdrawal of the request ends the review: § 860.250(a) lists the events (failure to respond completely to an additional-information request within 180 days; failure to respond to refusal-to-accept deficiencies within 180 days; denial of facility inspection; written notice of withdrawal) and § 860.250(b) requires FDA to notify the requester of withdrawal. None of these is a time limit for FDA to act on an accepted request.

6. LIMITS OF THIS DETERMINATION
- This answer is confined to 21 CFR Part 860 as fetched. The statutory counterpart in section 513(f)(2) of the FD&C Act was not among the fetched pages and is not quoted here; if a downstream user needs the statutory 120-day provision as a cross-check, that text must be pulled separately and compared. No conflict is expected, but it was not verified here.

7. ONE-LINE HOLDING
Under 21 CFR 860.230(a) and 860.240(a) as in force on 2026-11-21, FDA must notify the requester of acceptance within 15 days after receipt, and must issue the granting or declining order within 120 days after receipt; both periods run from the same receipt date, so the outside limit for the decision measured from receipt is 120 days.

question: Y163
answer:
REGULATORY DEADLINE CALCULATION — ICH E2A SEVEN-DAY EXPEDITED REPORTING

1. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS
- The case is assumed to meet the E2A criteria for expedited reporting as a fatal or life-threatening, serious, unexpected adverse drug reaction (SUSAR).
- Day 0 is the date the sponsor first receives information sufficient to meet the minimum reporting criteria: an identifiable patient, a suspect medicinal product, an identifiable reporting source, and a serious unexpected event for which, in a clinical investigation, a causal relationship cannot be ruled out. Day 0 is not counted as day 1.
- The E2A default periods are calendar days, not business days. Weekends and holidays count unless a binding local rule provides otherwise.
- No local jurisdictional variation or waiver is assumed. Binding local law may shorten or otherwise modify the E2A default and must be checked separately; where it does, the local requirement controls.

2. GOVERNING E2A RULE
ICH E2A §III.A.1 provides: 'Regulatory agencies should be notified (e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing) as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that a case qualifies, followed by as complete a report as possible within 8 additional calendar days. This report should include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products.'

3. CALCULATION
- Initial notification outer limit: end of day 7 after day 0, i.e. 7 calendar days.
- Follow-up outer limit: 8 additional calendar days after the date of the initial notification.
- If the sponsor uses the full initial period and notifies on day 7, the follow-up report that is as complete as possible is due by the end of day 15 after day 0: 7 + 8 = 15 calendar days.
- If the sponsor notifies earlier on day n (n ≤ 7), the follow-up is due by the end of day n + 8, which is earlier than day 15. Day 15 is therefore the outer limit measured from day 0 only when the full 7-day initial period is used.
- The 8-day follow-up period is not measured from day 0. It is anchored to the initial notification date.

Deadline table:
Day 0 — sponsor first knowledge; clock starts; day 0 is not counted as day 1.
Day 7 — outer limit for initial notification to regulatory agencies (7 calendar days).
Day 15 — outer limit for the follow-up report that is as complete as possible, if the initial notification is made on day 7 (8 additional calendar days).

4. CONTENT OF THE FOLLOW-UP REPORT
'As complete as possible' means the follow-up should provide the fullest available case information and, as E2A specifically requires, an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products. In practice this includes the complete case narrative, patient details, suspect and concomitant product details, event details and outcomes, reporter details, dates, causality assessment, relevant medical history, and the sponsor's benefit-risk assessment. If the initial notification was submitted on minimum criteria, the follow-up should fill the remaining data fields to the extent available.

5. PROCEDURE AND EVIDENCE
- Record the day 0 date and time, the source of the information, the minimum criteria met, and who determined that the case qualified.
- Submit the initial notification as soon as possible and no later than day 7; record the submission date and time and any regulatory acknowledgement or receipt.
- Submit the follow-up as soon as possible and no later than day n + 8 after the initial notification, where n is the day of initial notification; if n = 7, the outer limit is day 15 from day 0.
- If no additional information exists, document that the follow-up report is the complete report or that no further information is available. Do not silently omit the deadline.
- Retain the day 0 evidence and submission records for inspection.

6. BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
- This answer applies to the E2A seven-day rule for fatal or life-threatening serious unexpected ADRs. Serious unexpected ADRs that are neither fatal nor life-threatening follow the separate E2A 15-calendar-day initial reporting rule and are outside this ask.
- The 7-day and 15-day figures are outer limits, not targets; E2A requires notification 'as soon as possible.'
- If a local authority imposes a shorter period, the shorter period controls. If a local authority has a working-day rollover provision, apply that local provision only where it is binding; do not assume it under the E2A default.
