ANSWER: The next submission must carry serial number 018.

1. GOVERNING TEXT (supplied eCFR, 21 CFR 312.23(e), 'Numbering of IND submissions')
"Each submission relating to an IND is required to be numbered serially using a single, three-digit serial number. The initial IND is required to be numbered 000; each subsequent submission (e.g., amendment, report, or correspondence) is required to be numbered chronologically in sequence."
(Identical wording in ecfr.gov title-21 part-312 / § 312.23, govinfo CFR-2025-title21-vol5 § 312.23 PDF, and the CFR-2022 XML — sha256 247f94aced1a, c9fcf5cc6176, 6fe868becbda, 5b1f51ad2205 respectively.)

2. CALCULATION
- Base: the initial IND is numbered 000 (regulation fixes the origin at 000, not 0001).
- Each later submission increments by exactly one, chronologically, regardless of type (amendment, report, or correspondence are all expressly in scope of the same single sequence).
- 17 later submissions therefore occupy 001 through 017:

  | Position | Submission | Serial |
  |---|---|---|
  | 0 | Initial IND | 000 |
  | 1 | 1st later submission | 001 |
  | 2 | 2nd later submission | 002 |
  | … | … | … |
  | 16 | 16th later submission | 016 |
  | 17 | 17th later submission | 017 |
  | 18 | NEXT submission | 018 |

- General rule: serial = (number of submissions already made after the initial IND), zero-padded to three digits. Next serial = 17 + 1 = 18 → "018".
- Bound check: 018 is three digits and lies within the three-digit range 000–999; no rollover, no padding ambiguity.

3. RECONCILIATION WITH THE FORM FDA 1571 INSTRUCTIONS (flagged discrepancy, does not change the answer)
The Form FDA 1571 instruction pages (fda.gov/media/77596 and fda.gov/media/123543) state: initial IND = "Serial Number: 0000", next submission = "Serial Number: 0001", numbered consecutively thereafter. That is a four-digit rendering and is internally inconsistent with 312.23(e)'s "single, three-digit serial number." Under the form convention the 17 later submissions would run 0001–0017 and the next would be 0018 — four digits, i.e., not expressible as a three-digit number, which is precisely what the request asks for and what the regulation requires. The request directs the answer to the supplied eCFR text, so the regulation controls: 000 → 001…017 → 018. Recommend the sponsor's serial-number SOP follow 312.23(e) (000 base) and note the 1571 instruction text as a known FDA form inconsistency; do not let a CRO or eCTD tool default to the 0000 base.

4. CORRECTION TO THE PRIOR PROJECT ASSUMPTION
The project analysis assumed the initial IND is serial 0001 and the next submission is 0018. That base value is wrong under 312.23(e); the correct base is 000 and the correct next serial is 018.

5. SCOPE / CONDITIONS OF THE CONCLUSION
This holds because (a) all 17 intervening submissions were numbered serially in one chronological sequence as 312.23(e) requires (no gaps, no voids, no renumbering, no administrative cancellation), and (b) none of them was filed as a separate IND (a separate IND under 312.30 for exception-from-informed-consent emergency research would start its own 000 sequence). Before filing, confirm against FDA's acknowledgment/correspondence for the most recent submission that it was in fact serial 017; if the last acknowledged serial differs, the next serial is that serial plus one, still zero-padded to three digits.

6. ENTRY ON THE SUBMISSION
Form FDA 1571, Field 11 (SERIAL NUMBER): enter "018" (three digits, no prefix, no leading 'IND' in the field itself).

7. NOTE ON THE PROOF OF ABSENCE
The harness established that the literal string "019" does not appear in the eCFR § 312.23 page or the four other fetched sources. That is an absence of a specific literal string, not an absence of the governing rule: § 312.23(e) is present in full and fixes the numbering convention, from which 018 follows by the arithmetic in §2. The answer is therefore derived from the page, not reported as unstated, and ask 1 is neither blocked nor listed as not stated.

question: Y165
answer:
# Regulatory determination — custom device under FDCA § 520(b); 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E; as in force 2026-11-21

## 1. Question presented

A device meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA). Under 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, as in force on 2026-11-21, must its manufacturer submit a premarket notification at least 90 days before commercial distribution?

## 2. Answer

**No.** A device that is within the meaning of FDCA § 520(b) is exempt from the premarket notification requirements of 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, by operation of **21 CFR 807.85(a)**. The 90-day advance-submission obligation in **21 CFR 807.81(a)** therefore does not attach, and no 510(k) need be submitted before the device is introduced or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution.

The exemption is from Subpart E premarket notification **only**. It is not a general exemption from FDA device regulation (see § 5 below).

## 3. Controlling text relied on

**21 CFR 807.81(a)** (the rule that would otherwise apply):

> “Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria: (1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, (i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or (ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II. (2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section. (3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use…”

**21 CFR 807.85** (the exemption):

> “§ 807.85 Exemption from premarket notification.
> (a) A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
> (1) It is intended for use by a patient named in the order of the physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person); or
> (2) It is intended solely for use by a physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person) and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other physicians or dentists (or other specially qualified persons).
> (b) A distributor who places a device into commercial distribution for the first time under his own name and a repackager who places his own name on a device and does not change any other labeling or otherwise affect the device shall be exempted from the premarket notification requirements of this subpart if: (1) The device was in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976; or (2) A premarket notification submission was filed by another person.
> [42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016]”

## 4. Analysis

1. **The general rule is conditional, and the condition fails here.** § 807.81(a) obliges a 90-day advance premarket notification only for a device meeting one of the criteria in (a)(1)–(3). § 807.85(a) removes a § 520(b) custom device from “the premarket notification requirements of this subpart” — i.e., from Subpart E as a whole, including § 807.81.
2. **The statutory carve-out is not in § 807.81(b).** The exceptions listed in § 807.81(b) are a pending PMA/reclassification petition and a cleared PCCP. The custom-device carve-out operates independently, through § 807.85, and is keyed expressly to § 520(b).
3. **The premise satisfies the only regulatory condition.** § 807.85(a) applies “if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b).” The question stipulates that it is. Paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) restate the two statutory prongs — named-patient order, or physician/dentist-only use not generally available to or generally used by others — so a device meeting § 520(b) necessarily satisfies one of them.
4. **Result.** No premarket notification submission, and therefore no 90-day pre-submission interval, is required for this device on the stipulated facts. Because no submission is required, the corollary rule in Subpart E that marketing may not begin “until the applicant receives an order declaring a device substantially equivalent” is likewise inapplicable.

## 5. What the exemption does not reach

§ 807.85 exempts from Subpart E premarket notification only. A manufacturer of a custom device remains subject to, at minimum:

| Requirement | Status | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Establishment registration and device listing | Applies | 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart B (§ 807.20 et seq.) |
| Quality system regulation | Applies | 21 CFR Part 820 |
| Medical Device Reporting | Applies | 21 CFR Part 803 |
| Labeling | Applies | 21 CFR Part 801 |
| Unique Device Identification | Applies | 21 CFR Part 830 |
| Corrections and removals | Applies | 21 CFR Part 806 |
| Adulteration / misbranding prohibitions | Applies | FDCA §§ 501, 502 |
| Investigational device requirements, if used investigational | Applies | 21 CFR Part 812 |
| Premarket notification (510(k)) | **Exempt** | 21 CFR 807.85(a) |

A manufacturer must also not represent that the device has “FDA approval” or is “510(k) cleared” — Subpart E states that any representation creating an impression of official approval because of compliance with the premarket notification regulations is misleading and constitutes misbranding (21 CFR 807.97).

## 6. Conditions the manufacturer must keep satisfying

The exemption is not self-executing and is not permanent. To rely on it for each unit distributed, the manufacturer should be able to document:

- **The qualifying basis** — either (i) a physician’s or dentist’s order naming the patient and the device, or (ii) that the device is intended solely for use by the ordering practitioner and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other practitioners.
- **The statutory conditions added by FDASIA (Pub. L. 112-144, § 617, 2012)**, which are statutory rather than codified in § 807.85 and are therefore not visible in the regulatory text quoted above. These include the volume limitation on the physician-use prong — commonly stated as no more than **5 units per year of a device type** — and the manufacturer reporting obligation for custom devices. *Action item: verify the current codified text of FDCA § 520(b)(2)–(3) before relying on the exemption for a distribution program, because the question’s stipulation (“meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b)”) assumes these are satisfied but does not prove it.*
- **Non-general availability.** If the device is catalogued, advertised, or sold to the general practitioner market, the (a)(2) basis is lost and the device is no longer within § 520(b).

**Kill trigger:** if any element above fails for a given device or year, the exemption in § 807.85(a) is unavailable, and the device falls back under § 807.81(a): a premarket notification must be submitted **at least 90 days before** commercial distribution.

## 7. Currency and as-of date

- Text verified against the eCFR “current” edition of 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E (including the section-level pages for §§ 807.81 and 807.85), retrieved **2026-11-23T00:45:56Z** — two days after the 2026-11-21 as-of date — and cross-checked against the 2025 annual CFR print (CFR-2025-title21-vol8, Part 807 Subpart E). Both sources carry identical § 807.85 text.
- The source note for § 807.85 shows no amendment after **81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016**. § 807.81 carries a 2024 amendment (**89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024**) adding the PCCP exception at (b)(1)(ii); that amendment does not touch § 807.85.
- Residual risk: the retrieval reflects the codified text current as of 2026-11-23. If a rule amending § 807.85 or § 520(b) took effect on or before 2026-11-21 but is not yet reflected in the codified text, this answer would change. Nothing in the retrieved text signals such a change.

## 8. Note on the recorded proof of absence for ask 1

The harness searched the full text of the § 807.85 page for the literal strings “510(k)”, “PMN”, “90 days”, “90-day submission”, “Section 807.92”, and “21 CFR Part 807 Subpart E”, and found none. That is an artifact of the search terms, not silence on the question. Section 807.85 answers the question in its own operative words — “A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart” — which use neither “510(k)” nor “90 days”; the 90-day clock is in § 807.81(a), a different section of the same subpart, which was also retrieved and read in full and which is quoted verbatim in § 3 above. Accordingly ask 1 is answered (No) and is not listed as not stated.

## 9. Procedure the manufacturer should follow

1. Document the § 520(b) basis in writing for the specific device before first distribution: named-patient order (patient name, ordering practitioner, device specifications) **or** physician-only use with evidence the device is not generally available to or generally used by other practitioners.
2. Confirm the statutory conditions (volume limitation, custom-device reporting) are satisfied for the year of distribution; calendar the annual review.
3. Do **not** submit a 510(k), and do not state or imply FDA approval or clearance.
4. Complete establishment registration and device listing; maintain Part 820, Part 803, Part 830, Part 801, and Part 806 compliance.
5. Re-assess at every change of intended use, marketing method, or distribution volume. On any loss of the exemption, submit a premarket notification at least **90 days** before distribution and do not market until an order of substantial equivalence is received.
6. Retain the exemption-supporting records for the life of the distribution program and at least as long as the Part 820 record-retention periods require.

## 10. Limits of this determination

This answers the legal question on the stipulated fact that the device meets § 520(b). It does not verify that any particular device in fact qualifies, does not address state or foreign requirements, and does not constitute legal advice; a device-specific § 520(b) qualification review should precede reliance.

answer:
MEDICAL CONSULTANT ANSWER — Ask 2 (verdict)

VERDICT: No. The stated preference for TB blood tests (IGRAs) on the CDC 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis' page does NOT apply to a 4-year-old who received BCG, because the page's preference statement is expressly limited to people 5 years of age and older. The child meets the BCG condition but not the age condition; both are required.

1. GOVERNING TEXT ON THE NAMED PAGE
Page: 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis' — https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/ (page date stamp: Apr. 17, 2025; snapshot fetched 2026-11-23T00:48Z, sha256 9095c1db7f3e).
Verbatim, from the section 'TB blood tests (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])':
  'Only one visit is required to draw blood for the test. TB blood tests are the preferred method of TB testing for people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.'
This is the page's own statement of the preference, and it is age-qualified on its face. 'People 5 years of age and older' excludes a 4-year-old. The preference therefore does not reach this child.

2. CORROBORATION WITHIN THE SAME CDC 'CLINICAL TESTING AND DIAGNOSIS' SECTION (context, not the governing sentence)
- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/clinical-and-laboratory-diagnosis.html: 'Health care providers are encouraged to use TB blood tests to detect TB infection. TB blood tests are preferred for: People who have received the BCG vaccine and People who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation.' — and, in the same passage: 'Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age.' So even where the BCG indication is stated without an age qualifier, the same page supplies the age rule that displaces it for under-5s.
- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html: 'Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children. Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance on the use of TB blood tests in children.'
- Note a genuine tension in the source set, reported rather than smoothed over: the same TST page also says 'BCG vaccination does not induce positive results when TB blood tests are used. TB blood tests are the preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, including children.' That sentence is not age-qualified and pulls the other way. It does not change the verdict for this child, because (a) the named page's preference sentence is age-qualified at 5 years, and (b) the section's age-specific rule for children younger than 5 recommends the TB skin test as the method and routes any IGRA use in younger children to clinician judgement/AAP guidance. A 4-year-old falls squarely under the age-specific rule.

3. APPLICATION TO THE FACTS
- Age: 4 years → younger than 5 → outside the stated preference's age range.
- BCG history: present → satisfies the second condition, but conditions are conjunctive ('people 5 years of age and older who have received the BCG vaccine').
- Therefore: preference stated on the page = not applicable. This is a statement about the default CDC-preferred method, not a prohibition. The page nowhere says IGRA is contraindicated, unavailable, or inaccurate under age 5; it says TST is the recommended method for that age group and that some experts use blood tests in younger children, with AAP guidance available for consultation.
- BCG-specific handling on the page: 'The BCG vaccine may cause a false-positive TB skin test reaction. There is no reliable way to distinguish a positive TB skin test reaction caused by BCG vaccination from a reaction caused by true TB infection. Interpretation of the TB skin test reaction is the same for people who have had BCG vaccination as it is for those who have not.' (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html). Practical consequence: if TST is used in this BCG-vaccinated child, do not 'adjust' or discount the induration for BCG — read it by the standard criteria — and treat any positive result as requiring the full medical evaluation (history, physical, repeat test as indicated, chest radiograph, specimen collection as indicated).

4. WHAT APPLIES INSTEAD — CLINICAL PROCEDURE FOR THIS CHILD
Step 1. Default method for a 4-year-old per CDC: Mantoux tuberculin skin test, with reading and interpretation at 48–72 hours by a trained reader; schedule the return visit at the time of placement (the page notes one advantage of IGRA is that only one visit is required, which is exactly why the 'might be less likely to return for reading' indication exists — if this child's family is at high risk of not returning, that is a documented reason to discuss IGRA).
Step 2. If IGRA is being considered for this 4-year-old (e.g., high likelihood of missed TST reading, clinical concern about BCG-induced TST reactivity, or family preference), treat it as a clinician-discretion decision informed by AAP guidance, and document the rationale. Do not describe it to the family as 'the CDC-preferred test' for this child.
Step 3. Confirm the specific assay's FDA-approved age range and the performing laboratory's validated age range before ordering, since the CDC page does not address test-specific minimum ages. The page lists the two commercially available assays as QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) and T-SPOT.TB test (T-Spot) and states that FDA has approved these two; it does not state an age limit for either.
Step 4. Regardless of test chosen: a negative result does not rule out infection or disease. Per the page set, children under 5 with a known exposure should receive window prophylaxis even with an initial negative test if fewer than 8–10 weeks have passed since last exposure (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html). If the child has symptoms of TB disease, do not wait for immunodiagnostic results before pursuing chest imaging and microbiologic evaluation.
Step 5. Revisit the question at age 5: once the child is 5 years of age or older and has received BCG, the named page's preference for TB blood tests applies directly.

5. SCOPE LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
- The answer is strictly about what the named page states; it is not a recommendation that this child receive or not receive any specific test. Test selection remains a clinical decision with the treating provider, informed by exposure history, likelihood of TST return, assay availability/cost, and AAP guidance where relevant.
- The page does not address BCG-vaccinated children as a separate category from BCG-vaccinated adults beyond the age qualifier, and it does not state an assay-specific minimum age.
- Provenance assumption, stated openly: the ask specifies the page 'available on 2026-11-21'; the retrieved snapshot is timestamped 2026-11-23T00:48Z. The page carries an 'Apr. 17, 2025' content date and no intervening revision is indicated, so the snapshot is treated as the version available on 2026-11-21. If a revision landed between 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-23, this verdict should be re-checked against the 2026-11-21 capture.

6. NOT-STATED DETERMINATION (recorded so reviewers can see the reasoning)
not_stated is empty. The harness proof of absence supplied for ask 2 concerns https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html (33,773 characters, sha256 171f6557d84e) and searched for 'IGRA (Interferon-gamma Release Assay)', 'TST (Tuberculin Skin Test)', 'BCG-vaccinated', 'preferred', and 'children >=2 years'. That is a different page from the one ask 2 names, and the searched strings are not the words in which this answer is printed. Moreover the named page affirmatively answers ask 2, so there is nothing to report as 'the page states none,' and nothing is blocked.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR THE RECORD: On the CDC 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis' page (Apr. 17, 2025 version, available 2026-11-21), the stated preference for TB blood tests is limited to 'people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine'; a 4-year-old BCG recipient is below that age threshold, so the preference does not apply — CDC's recommended method for children younger than 5 is the TB skin test, with IGRA in younger children left to expert/clinician judgement and AAP guidance.

# Guideline identification for the primary-care hypertension pathway

## 1. Answers (for direct use in the pathway header and citation block)

**Ask 1 — which NICE guideline covers the scope.**
NICE guideline **NG136**, *Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management*.
- Reference number: **NG136**
- Published: **28 August 2019**
- Last updated: **26 February 2026**
- ISBN: 978-1-4731-9329-1
- Source: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136 (fetched 2026-11-23T00:49:27Z, sha256 592a154eb06d)

Scope match is explicit, not inferred. NG136's overview states verbatim:

> "This guideline covers identifying and treating primary hypertension (high blood pressure) in people aged 18 and over, including people with type 2 diabetes."

The Context chapter repeats it: "The guideline covers adults (over 18 years) with suspected or diagnosed hypertension, including those with type 2 diabetes." The recommendations chapter adds: "The recommendations on measuring blood pressure and diagnosing hypertension in this guideline apply to all adults, including those with type 2 diabetes." So 'adults with type 2 diabetes' is inside NG136's scope, not a separate guideline the team must bolt on.

**Ask 2 — which earlier NICE hypertension guideline it says it updates and replaces.**
**CG127.**

NG136 states it verbatim on its overview page:

> "This guideline updates and replaces NICE guideline CG127."

Source: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136 (fetched 2026-11-23T00:49:27Z, sha256 592a154eb06d)

The NG136 PDF carries the same relationship in NICE's standard replacement wording:

question: Y168
answer:
QUESTION 1 — Is 'the research is minimal risk' alone a sufficient reason to enroll a person in an FDA-regulated clinical investigation without informed consent under 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21?

ANSWER: No. Verdict identifier: INSUFFICIENT.

1. The baseline rule makes consent mandatory unless a listed exception applies. 21 CFR 50.20: 'Except as provided in §§ 50.22, 50.23, and 50.24, no investigator may involve a human being as a subject in research covered by these regulations unless the investigator has obtained the legally effective informed consent of the subject or the subject's legally authorized representative.' Minimal risk is not itself one of the three listed exceptions; it is one element inside one of them (§50.22). A fact pattern that stops at 'minimal risk' therefore never leaves the baseline rule of §50.20.

2. The one exception keyed to minimal risk is conjunctive, not a single test. 21 CFR 50.22 (added by 88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023) permits the IRB to 'approve an informed consent procedure that does not include or that alters some or all of the elements of informed consent set forth in § 50.25(a) and (b), or [to] waive the requirement to obtain informed consent, provided the IRB finds and documents the following:
   (a) The clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects;
   (b) The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration;
   (c) If the clinical investigation involves using identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens, the clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without using such information or biospecimens in an identifiable format;
   (d) The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects; and
   (e) Whenever appropriate, the subjects or legally authorized representatives will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation.'
   Minimal risk is subparagraph (a) only. On the face of the text, (b), (c) (where identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens are used), (d) and (e) are independent, cumulative requirements. An investigator who offers only minimal risk has established, at most, one of five findings, and has established none of them in the only forum that counts (see point 3).

3. The investigator is not the decision-maker. Section 50.22 vests the authority in 'The IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation,' and requires that the IRB 'finds and documents' each element. Two consequences follow: (i) an investigator's own conclusion that the research is minimal risk has no legal effect on the consent requirement; and (ii) the findings must be documented. An enrollment made on the investigator's unilateral minimal-risk judgment is a violation of §50.20, not an exercise of §50.22, and it also exposes the IRB approval and the IND/IDE to challenge.

4. Minimal risk cannot bear the weight even where it is correctly found. Each of the following overlays applies independently of §50.22(a):
   - Practicability (§50.22(b)): if consent could practicably be obtained, the waiver is unavailable no matter how low the risk.
   - Identifiable data/biospecimens (§50.22(c)): a separate practicability finding is required if the research uses identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens in identifiable form.
   - Rights and welfare (§50.22(d)): a distinct, forward-looking finding about the effect of the waiver itself.
   - Debriefing (§50.22(e)): post-participation information 'whenever appropriate.'
   - Children (Subpart D): even where no greater than minimal risk is presented, §50.51 provides that children may be involved 'only if the IRB finds that: (a) No greater than minimal risk to children is presented; and (b) Adequate provisions are made for soliciting the assent of the children and the permission of their parents or guardians as set forth in § 50.55.' So for children, minimal risk is expressly paired with — and never substitutes for — assent and parental permission. §§50.52 and 50.53 similarly couple risk findings with §50.55 assent/permission duties. A §50.22 waiver does not displace Subpart D.
   - Emergency research (§50.24): the emergency-research exception runs on its own criteria — subjects 'in a life-threatening situation, available treatments are unproven or unsatisfactory,' infeasibility of consent, and the additional protections of §50.24(a)(7), including community consultation ((a)(7)(i)), prior public disclosure ((a)(7)(ii)), post-completion disclosure ((a)(7)(iii)), and an independent data monitoring committee ((a)(7)(iv)). Minimal risk is neither a trigger nor a shortcut there; a low-risk emergency study still has to satisfy §50.24 in full if that is the exception relied on.
   - §50.23: the separate 'Exception from general requirements' likewise stands on its own terms and is not satisfied by a minimal-risk characterization.

5. Bottom line on Question 1. 'Minimal risk' is a necessary condition for a §50.22 waiver and never a sufficient one, and in no case is the investigator the actor who may rely on it. The statement 'this investigation may enroll a person without informed consent solely because the research is minimal risk' is incorrect as a matter of law under Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21. The correct formulation is: the IRB responsible for the investigation may waive or alter informed consent only if it finds and documents all of §50.22(a)-(e), and must additionally secure Subpart D assent/permission where children are involved; absent such findings and documentation, §50.20 requires legally effective informed consent.

QUESTION 2 — How does 21 CFR Part 50 define 'minimal risk'?

ANSWER (verbatim, 21 CFR 50.3, Definitions): 'Minimal risk means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests.'

Parsing the definition, element by element:
- Two dimensions, both required: 'the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort.' A very unlikely serious harm and a very likely trivial discomfort are each assessed on both axes, not on one alone.
- It is a comparative, not an absolute, standard. There is no numeric probability, no severity ceiling, and no list of permitted procedures. The definition supplies a comparator and nothing more.
- The comparator is double: (i) risks 'ordinarily encountered in daily life,' or (ii) risks of 'routine physical or psychological examinations or tests.' Either benchmark may be used; the regulation does not rank them.
- The phrase 'anticipated in the research' fixes the object of the assessment: the harms and discomforts the research as proposed actually presents, not the subject's underlying disease risk and not speculative harms.
- The phrase 'not greater in and of themselves' isolates the research contribution: the research procedures are compared to the benchmark on their own account, rather than being netted against the prospect of therapeutic benefit. A study with favorable benefit-risk can still involve more than minimal risk; conversely, a minimal-risk study may offer no benefit at all.
- The definition is subject-relative in application: the benchmark is what is ordinarily encountered by the population being enrolled, which is why a procedure that is routine for one population may not be minimal risk for another. The definition itself states the standard; the population-specific application is the IRB's finding.
- Functionally, minimal risk is a threshold/eligibility concept. In Part 50 it does work in §50.22(a) (waiver or alteration of consent), §50.51(a) (children, no greater than minimal risk), and by contrast in §§50.52 and 50.53 ('more than minimal risk,' and 'a minor increase over minimal risk' in §50.53(a)). It is not, anywhere in Part 50, a free-standing authorization to dispense with consent.

HOW TO APPLY IT — a checklist an investigator or IRB administrator can execute directly:
1. Identify the population and the enrollment context (adult able to consent; adult unable to consent; child; life-threatening emergency). The applicable exception differs and §50.22 is not a universal key.
2. Identify the exception being invoked, by section: §50.22 (minimal risk waiver/alteration), §50.23 (exception from general requirements), or §50.24 (emergency research). Do not blend them.
3. If §50.22 is invoked, build the record for each element separately and in writing:
   (a) Minimal risk — state the comparator used (daily life or routine examinations/tests), the specific procedures assessed, and why probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort are not greater than the comparator for this population.
   (b) Practicability — document why the research cannot practicably be carried out with the requested waiver or alteration (e.g., the population cannot be reached, refusal/selection bias would destroy validity, procedures are inseparable from the data collection). Assertion alone is not documentation.
   (c) Identifiable information/biospecimens — if applicable, a separate finding that the research cannot practicably be carried out without using them in identifiable form. If not applicable, say so expressly in the record.
   (d) Rights and welfare — a finding about the effect of the waiver itself on subjects' rights and welfare.
   (e) Debriefing — a finding that additional pertinent information will be provided after participation whenever appropriate, or a reasoned statement of why it is not appropriate.
4. If children are involved, add the Subpart D overlay: §50.51(a) risk finding plus §50.51(b) adequate provisions for assent of the children and permission of parents/guardians under §50.55. Where risk exceeds minimal risk, use §§50.52/50.53 and note §50.53(a)'s 'minor increase over minimal risk' ceiling.
5. If the context is a life-threatening emergency, use §50.24 and build the record for each finding in §50.24(a), including the physician concurrence required by the introductory text of §50.24(a) and the additional protections of §50.24(a)(7)(i)-(iv). Also note §50.24's separate-IND/IDE requirement and the obligation, described in the §50.24 text, that the IRB ensure procedures exist to inform the subject (or a legally authorized representative, or a family member) at the earliest feasible opportunity.
6. Do not enroll anyone on the strength of step 3(a) alone. Enrollment may proceed without consent only after the IRB has made and documented the complete set.

COMMON MISREADINGS THIS ANALYSIS CORRECTS:
- Treating 'minimal risk' as a waiver category. It is one criterion within §50.22, and §50.22 is an IRB power, not an investigator power.
- Treating §50.22 as satisfying Subpart D. It does not; §50.51(b) assent and parental permission still apply.
- Treating low risk as a substitute for the §50.24 emergency criteria. It is not; §50.24 does not turn on minimal risk.
- Reading the §50.3 definition as a numeric threshold. It is comparative only; the regulation supplies no number.
- Reading 'not greater in and of themselves' as permitting netting against anticipated benefit. It does not; the research procedures are compared to the benchmark on their own account.

CURRENCY AND SOURCES. The text relied on is the eCFR 'current' text of §§50.20, 50.22, 50.24 and 50.51 and the 2025 edition of 21 CFR Part 50 (govinfo), as fetched 2026-11-23. Section 50.22 carries the source note '[88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023]' and §50.20 carries the amendment note '88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023'; §50.24 carries '[61 FR 51528, Oct. 2, 1996]'. All are effective well before 2026-11-21 and therefore in force on that date, including the minimal-risk consent exception. The §50.3 definition quoted above appears in the full text of Part 50 as published.

SCOPE. This is an interpretation of 21 CFR Part 50 only, as requested. It does not address state law, 21 CFR Part 56 (IRB organization and operation), Parts 312/812 (IND/IDE mechanics), or non-FDA regimes such as the Common Rule, and it is not an approval of any specific protocol; the §50.22 and Subpart D findings are the responsible IRB's to make and document.

DETERMINATION: UHECR ENERGY THRESHOLD IN THE 2024 PDG COSMIC-RAY REVIEW

Question as posed: (1) what energy threshold does the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review use to define ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs); (2) is that threshold inclusive or exclusive.

Source pinned. '2024 PDG cosmic-ray review' is taken to mean Sec. 30, 'Cosmic Rays', of the Review of Particle Physics 2024 (S. Navas et al., Particle Data Group, Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)), authored October 2023 by J. Alvarez-Muniz, Z. Cao, U.F. Katz, P. Mertsch and C. Spiering, published as the standalone chapter https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf (37 pages, 123,924 characters, fetched 2026-11-23T00:53:48Z, sha256 c8f0620d58d3, running date '19th September, 2024'). Corroborating 2024 artifacts were also read: the full compendium db2024.pdf (288 pages, sha256 fffa63acbd33), the Highlights sheet (sha256 6e206d3bc575), the chapter 'Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics' (sha256 92b8d56c8743), and a 2024-25 preprint that cites the chapter, arXiv:2502.11834 (sha256 dd4de209e8b5).

RESULT FOR ASK 1 (threshold value): NOT STATED IN THE PAGE. Sec. 30 never defines UHECRs by an energy threshold. It uses 'UHECR'/'UHE-CR' as an established label and attaches numbers only to other, distinct quantities. The relevant verbatim sentences are:
  - 'Between hundreds of MeV and at least a few PeV, CRs are believed to be of galactic origin; above a few EeV, the sources are most likely extra-galactic.' — a statement about probable source populations, hedged ('a few EeV'), and not a definition of the UHECR class.
  - 'UHECRs are subject to the GZK effect, the energy loss of protons and heavier nuclei in interactions with the cosmic background. This imposes a horizon to possible sources of ~250 Mpc for protons and Fe nuclei ... at energies above ~50EeV.' — 50 EeV is attached to the GZK horizon, not to the definition of UHECR.
  - 'The suppression of the spectrum starting around 50EeV.' — a spectral feature, not a class definition.
  - 'The Pierre Auger Collaboration has discovered a large-scale dipolar anisotropy at energies above 8EeV ... evidencing the extra-galactic origin of UHECRs above this energy threshold.' — this is the closest the chapter comes to a threshold tied to UHECRs, but it is explicitly a threshold for the dipole anisotropy / extragalactic-origin claim, and it is phrased 'above 8EeV'. Quoting it as 'the UHECR energy threshold' would misrepresent the sentence, so it is not used.
  - Other uses of the acronym carry no energy at all, e.g. 'from the cascade of very-high-energy gamma rays and UHECRs are not ruled out ...'.
Evidence of absence: the full 37-page text was searched and contains none of the strings a UHECR threshold definition would be printed with — 'E > 10^18 eV', 'E >= 1 EeV', 'UHECR energy > 10^18 eV', 'Ultra-high-energy cosmic ray threshold: 10^18 eV', 'Threshold: >10^18 eV', 'E > 1 EeV'. The same negative result holds for db2024.pdf, the Highlights sheet and arXiv:2502.11834. Ask 1 is therefore recorded as not stated, with no figure. The widely quoted 10^18 eV / 1 EeV figure is general community usage; it is not text in this review, and asserting it (or asserting an inequality on it) would be an invented attribution.

RESULT FOR ASK 2 (inclusive vs exclusive): NOT STATED, as a direct consequence of ask 1. With no threshold sentence in the chapter there is no '>=' or '>' to report. The full text was searched for 'exclusive (>)', 'inclusive (>=)', 'threshold defined as greater than 10^18 eV (exclusive)', 'threshold defined as at least 10^18 eV (inclusive)', 'exclusive cutoff' and 'inclusive cutoff'; none occurs, in the chapter or in arXiv:2502.11834. No verdict is asserted. The word 'inclusive' does occur in the 2024 corpus, but only as Sec. 49 reaction headings ('49.5.2 Inclusive reactions', '49.6.1 Single production with semi-invisible final state', '49.6.2 Pair production with semi-invisible final states') in db2024.pdf, which are unrelated to cosmic rays.

QUARANTINED — ADJACENT PDG 2024 MATERIAL THAT IS NOT THE ANSWER. Recorded only so that a later editor does not mistake it for a result. The separate chapter 36, 'Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics' (https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-particle-detectors-non-accel.pdf), does attach energy conditions to ultra-high-energy particles: 'An extensive air shower (EAS) is produced by the interactions of ultra high-energy (E > 10^17 eV) subatomic particles in the stratosphere and upper troposphere'; 'Cosmogenic neutrinos are produced when ultra-high energy (UHE) protons with energy E > 5x10^19 eV interact with photons from the CMBR ...'; and 'With energies extending beyond 10^20 eV, ultra high energy cosmic rays (UHE-CRs) are the highest energy subatomic particles known to exist.' These sentences (a) belong to a different review chapter, not the cosmic-ray review the request names; (b) are mutually inconsistent as definitions — an EAS-production condition at 10^17 eV, a cosmogenic-neutrino proton condition at 5x10^19 eV, and a lower-bound-free 'beyond 10^20 eV' remark; and (c) therefore cannot be transferred to Sec. 30. They appear in this summary as context only and are deliberately excluded from results.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE THE GAP (for a follow-up iteration with the printed source): (i) check the paginated Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 version of Sec. 30 for a definition sentence lost in PDF text extraction (equation objects, figure captions, or table notes); (ii) check whether the Booklet's acronym/glossary table carries a UHECR entry; (iii) if the requester will accept a different PDG artifact, the chapter-36 sentences above are quotable, but they answer a different question (detector context) and must be cited as such, not as 'the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review'.

FINAL STATEMENT: For the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review (Sec. 30, rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf), the energy threshold defining UHECRs is not stated, and consequently no inclusive/exclusive determination can be given from that source. Asks 1 and 2 are recorded as not stated against that page; nothing is blocked, because the absence itself is the evidenced answer.

question: Y171
answer:
# Mars surface pressure at mean radius and seasonal range — NASA Mars Fact Sheet, reference date 2026-11-21

## 1. Answer

The NASA NSSDCA **Mars Fact Sheet** states, verbatim, in its *Martian Atmosphere* block:

> Surface pressure:  6.36 mb at mean radius (variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season)
> [6.9 mb to 9 mb (Viking 1 Lander site)]

So:

| Ask | Value as stated by the sheet | Unit | SI equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Surface pressure at mean radius | **6.36** | mb (= hPa = mbar) | **636 Pa** (0.636 kPa, 6.36 hPa, 0.00636 bar) |
| 2. Seasonal range | **4.0 to 8.7** | mb | **400 Pa to 870 Pa** |

Both figures are transcribed, not recomputed. `mb` in this fact sheet means millibar, numerically identical to hPa; the sheet does not use Pa anywhere in this block.

## 2. Provenance and version check against 2026-11-21

- Page: `https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/marsfact.html` (NSSDCA Planetary Fact Sheets, curator Dr. David R. Williams).
- Page self-reported stamp: `Last Updated: 19 May 2025, DRW`.
- Retrieved: 2026-11-23T00:56:28Z; sha256 of fetched text `366b0ce9b69c` (harness prefix), full-text length 6,419 characters.
- **Why this is the 2026-11-21 version:** the content's last-update stamp (19 May 2025) precedes the reference date by ~18 months, so the retrieved text is the same revision that was published on 2026-11-21. The only residual risk is an edit landing in the 2-day window between the reference date and the fetch; the page carries no revision newer than May 2025, so no evidence of such an edit exists.
- Note the sheet is a *living* page with no DOI/versioned archive. For traceability in the pressure model, cite the stamp + fetch timestamp + sha256 above, not just the URL.

## 3. Adjudication of the harness proofs of absence (why these asks are *not* in `not_stated`)

The harness recorded absence proofs for asks 1 and 2 on all six pages, searching for strings such as `Surface pressure (mean) = 610 Pa`, `Mean surface pressure: 610 Pa`, `P0 ≈ 610 Pa`, `Surface pressure (mean) ≈ 0.610 kPa`, `Seasonal pressure range: 4–9 mbar`, `Seasonal range: 400–900 Pa`, `Seasonal variation in pressure: 400 Pa – 900 Pa`. All of those are **paraphrases denominated in Pa/kPa or written in symbolic notation**. The fact sheet never uses those forms: it reports in **mb** under the label **`Surface pressure:`**, and expresses seasonality as the parenthetical **`(variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season)`** rather than as a phrase like "seasonal range".

Consequently the proofs establish *absence of the paraphrase strings*, not *absence of the statement*. The statement is present verbatim in the quoted page text (section 1). Per the rule that an ask goes into `not_stated` only when the page states none, **neither ask is in `not_stated`**, and the summary names the page as the one that does state them.

## 4. Pressure-model input card

```
# mars_pressure_input.yaml  — preliminary lander model, global datum
source:
  document: NASA NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet
  url: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/marsfact.html
  page_last_updated: 2025-05-19
  reference_date: 2026-11-21
  retrieved: 2026-11-23T00:56:28Z
  sha256_prefix: 366b0ce9b69c
  quoted_text: >
    Surface pressure:  6.36 mb at mean radius (variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb
    depending on season) [6.9 mb to 9 mb (Viking 1 Lander site)]

pressure:
  datum: mean radius            # sheet's wording: "at mean radius"
  datum_radius_km: 3389.5       # volumetric mean radius, same sheet, bulk-parameters block
  mean:
    value: 636.0
    unit: Pa                    # transcribed as 6.36 mb; 1 mb = 100 Pa
  seasonal_envelope:
    min: 400.0                  # transcribed as 4.0 mb
    max: 870.0                  # transcribed as 8.7 mb
    unit: Pa
    cause: seasonal CO2 condensation/sublimation cycle on the polar caps (global average)
    representation: min_max_envelope   # NOT a time series; sheet gives no phase/season mapping

supporting_constants:           # same page, same block — use for elevation transfer
  scale_height_km: 11.0
  surface_density_kg_m3: 0.016  # sheet gives ~0.016 +/- 0.006
  mean_temperature_K: 214.0
  surface_gravity_m_s2: 3.73

excluded:
  - value: 6.9-9 mb (690-900 Pa)
    reason: bracketed Viking 1 Lander site figure, site-specific, not the global seasonal range
```

**Envelope representation.** The sheet supplies a min/max only; it gives no seasonal phase, no sol-of-year mapping, and no functional form. Use it as a **design envelope** (min/max bounds on a uniform prior or a hard clamp), not as a time-varying profile. If a time series is needed later, it must come from a different source (surface-mission meteorology or a Mars climate model); the fact sheet cannot supply it.

**Derived envelope descriptors (computed, for the model's convenience):**
- max/min ratio = 870/400 = **2.175**
- geometric (log-)mean = sqrt(400 × 870) = **589.9 Pa** — slightly below the stated 636 Pa mean, consistent with a right-skewed envelope
- log half-amplitude = ½·ln(2.175) = **±0.389** (multiplicative factor 1.475 / 0.678 about the log-mean)
- linear half-range about the stated mean: 636 − 400 = 236 Pa low, 870 − 636 = 234 Pa high

## 5. Datum handling for a lander site (datum is mean radius, not local surface)

The 6.36 mb / 400–870 mb figures are referenced to **mean radius (3389.5 km)**, i.e. the global zero-elevation datum — **not** to a landing-site surface. The sheet also brackets a site value (Viking 1, 6.9–9 mb), which is evidence that site pressure departs from the mean-radius figure. Transfer to a site of elevation *h* (km, positive up, relative to the mean-radius datum):

```
p_site = p_mean_radius · exp(−h / H),  H = 11.0 km
```

Apply the same factor to the envelope to keep it consistent (the factor is elevation-only; it does not model the seasonal phase).

*Illustrative worked case* — assume a site at h = −2.6 km (below the datum):
- factor = exp(2.6/11.0) = **1.2666**
- mean → 636 × 1.2666 = **805.6 Pa**

## 6. Disambiguation traps a downstream reader will hit

1. **The Planetary Fact Sheet table gives Mars `Surface Pressure (bars) = 0.01`.** That is the same quantity rounded to two decimal places in bars (0.00636 bar → 0.01 bar), **not** a competing measurement. 3. **`mb` ≠ `mbar` ≠ `bar`.** 6.36 mb = 6.36 mbar = 6.36 hPa = 636 Pa = 0.00636 bar. A factor-of-1000 slip (6.36 bar) is the most likely transcription error.

| Mean inside envelope | 400 ≤ 636 ≤ 870 | — | — | ✓ |

These confirm the transcribed 6.36 mb is consistent with the sheet's own companion constants (11.0 km scale height, ~214 K, ~0.016 kg/m³) — i.e. the value has been read correctly and not mis-scaled.

## 8. Bottom line for the model

- **Ask 1:** surface pressure at mean radius = **6.36 mb = 636 Pa** (global datum, mean radius 3389.5 km).
- **Ask 2:** seasonal range = **4.0 to 8.7 mb = 400 to 870 Pa**, global average, driven by the CO2 cap cycle; supplied as a min/max envelope only.

# Answer

**H0 = (67.4 ± 0.5) km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹** (base-ΛCDM; ±0.5 is the 68% / 1σ marginalized uncertainty, the paper's native convention).

## Verbatim source text
The abstract of Planck Collaboration VI, *Planck 2018 results: VI. Cosmological parameters*, A&A **641**, A6 (2020), DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201833910, arXiv:1807.06209, states (quoted exactly as fetched):

> "Assuming the base-ΛCDM cosmology, the inferred (model-dependent) late-Universe parameters are: Hubble constant H0 = (67.4 ± 0.5) km s-1 Mpc-1; matter density parameter ωm = 0.315 ± 0.007; and matter fluctuation amplitude σ8 = 0.811 ± 0.006."

Source of the quoted abstract: https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/planck-2018-results-vi-cosmological-parameters/ (record for A&A 641, A6, DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201833910; abstract text reproduced there).

## Independent corroboration
A separate fetched paper (arXiv:2606.02097v1, §2.1 "Planck-Anchored Baseline Cosmology") restates the same constraint when citing Planck 2018 VI:

> "...assuming spatial flatness (Ωk = 0), it reported Hubble constant H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and Ωm = 0.315 ± 0.007."

Two independent fetched sources agree digit-for-digit on 67.4 ± 0.5, so the transcription is not a single-source artefact.

## What is being quoted, and what is not
- The abstract reports **one** base-ΛCDM H0. It is the model-dependent late-Universe parameter derived from the base-ΛCDM fit to the Planck CMB likelihood (the baseline TT,TE,EE+lowE data combination in the paper's language). The abstract does **not** quote a separate H0 for lensing or BAO variants, so there is no ambiguity about which abstract number is meant.
- For completeness only (these are **not** the answer to this ask, and are not in the abstract): the paper's parameter tables give H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ for TT,TE,EE+lowE and H0 = 67.66 ± 0.53 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ when lensing is added. The abstract's 67.4 ± 0.5 is the rounded form of the former; the two are consistent, not contradictory.
- The value 73.45 ± 1.66 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ that appears in the same parameter-table document is the *Riess et al. 2018 SHOES* measurement used as an external dataset, not a Planck inference, and must not be reported here.

## Uncertainty convention
Planck VI reports ± values as 68% confidence (1σ) marginalized limits from the MCMC chains (the abstract and Tables 1–2 use this convention). "±0.5" is therefore a 1σ uncertainty, not a 95% bound. (A 95% table exists separately in the Planck Legacy Archive and would give a wider interval; it is not the abstract's convention.)

## Unit note (known typo in the source)
The abstract as printed/rendered reads "km s-1 **Mpc**-1"; the correct and intended unit, used throughout the paper's tables ("H0 ... Current expansion rate in km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹"), is **km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹**. I report the standard unit and flag the typo rather than propagating it.

## Version / citation notes
- arXiv:1807.06209 and the published A&A 641, A6 (2020) version carry the same abstract value, 67.4 ± 0.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹; no version discrepancy affects the answer.
- Suggested citation for the answer: Planck Collaboration VI, A&A 641, A6 (2020), arXiv:1807.06209, abstract.

## One-line restatement for downstream use
> Base-ΛCDM Hubble constant from the Planck 2018 VI abstract: **H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹** (1σ).

question: Y174
answer:
Equatorial-minus-polar radius difference for Earth

Given (NASA Earth Fact Sheet):
  equatorial radius a = 6378.137 km
  polar radius      b = 6356.752 km

Requested quantity: a - b, in km.

Calculation (exact, no rounding needed):
  a - b = 6378.137 - 6356.752
        = 21.385

Step-by-step for audit:
  6378.137 - 6356.000 = 22.137
  22.137 - 0.752     = 21.385

Result: 21.385 km (approximately 21.4 km).

Notes on conventions and precision:
  - Sign: the quantity is defined as equatorial minus polar. Because a > b for Earth, the result is positive; the opposite ordering would give -21.385 km.
  - Precision: both inputs are stated to three decimal places (1 m), and the difference of the stated decimals is exact at three decimal places, so the reported value carries the same precision as the inputs and no rounding rule needs to be invoked.
  - Sanity bounds: the difference must lie between 0 and either radius; 21.385 km is far below both 6356.752 km and 6378.137 km, as required. As a fraction of the equatorial radius it is 21.385 / 6378.137 = 0.3353 %, i.e. about 1/298, which is the expected scale of Earth's flattening.

Independent cross-check via flattening (same fact sheet):
  1/f = 298.257  =>  f = 1/298.257 = 0.00335281
  a - b = a·f = 6378.137 × 0.00335281 = 21.3847 km ≈ 21.385 km
  This agrees with the direct subtraction to the stated precision.

Answer to the ask: 21.385 km.

question: Y177
answer:
# 1. Answer

| ask | value | unit |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Value of S to enter | **110.4** | K |
| 2. By how much the document's value was too small | **0.4** | K |

Derived printed value: 110.4 - 0.4 = **110 K** (U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976, Table 2, B. Category II Constants, p. 2). The correction is therefore +0.4 K, i.e. +0.364% relative to 110 K.

# 2. Source of the correction

Errata sheet distributed with the NTRS record 19770009539 (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19770009539/downloads/19770009539.pdf), item 2 of the list of errors in Table 2, B. Category II Constants, p. 2:

> "2) The value for Sutherland's constant S is too small by 0.4. It should be 110.4 Kelvin."

Provenance note (record it in the commit message): the errata text is a correspondent's (Yekta Gursel) itemised correction list addressed to NASA STI and hosted with the NTRS record, not a separately typeset NASA corrigendum. It is the errata NASA distributes for that document ID and is unambiguous for this constant. Two pages in the grounding do **not** contain it and must not be cited as the source: the NTRS landing page for the record is metadata only, and the widely used Fortran reference implementation (pdas.com/programs/atmos76.f90, v0.91) already hard-codes `SUTH = 110.4` but never states the errata. The listing is useful only as corroboration that 110.4 is the value in operational use.

# 3. Where the constant lives and how it is consumed

In the reference implementation the constant block is

    REAL,PARAMETER:: BETAVISC = 1.458E-6   ! viscosity term, N s/(m^2 sqrt(K))
    REAL,PARAMETER:: SUTH     = 110.4      ! Sutherland's constant, K

and it is consumed only by the viscosity function:

    Viscosity = BETAVISC*SQRT(t*t*t)/(t + SUTH)

    mu = beta * T^(3/2) / (T + S),   T in K,  mu in kg m^-1 s^-1 (= Pa s),  beta = 1.458e-6

S appears nowhere else in the model. **Do not touch the 245.4 in the thermal-conductivity fit** `kt = 2.64638e-3 * T^(3/2) / (T + 245.4*10^(-12/T))`; that is an unrelated empirical coefficient, not S. Do not change `BETAVISC` (1.458e-6) either.

# 4. Patch

## 4.1 Fortran (atmos76.f90 and forks)

    ! --- U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976, Table 2 (Category II), as corrected ---
    ! Errata for NTRS 19770009539: the printed S = 110 K is too small by 0.4 K;
    ! the correct value is 110.4 K. See errata sheet, item 2, Table 2, Cat. II.
    REAL,PARAMETER:: BETAVISC = 1.458E-6   ! N s /(m^2 sqrt(K))
    REAL,PARAMETER:: SUTH     = 110.4      ! Sutherland's constant, K  (was 110.0)

    FUNCTION Viscosity(t)
      REAL,INTENT(IN):: t          ! temperature, K
      REAL:: Viscosity             ! kg/(m s) = Pa s
      Viscosity = BETAVISC*SQRT(t*t*t)/(t + SUTH)
    END FUNCTION Viscosity

Note: the upstream pdas.com v0.91 listing already carries 110.4, so the defect exists only in forks/vendored copies that pinned the printed table value of 110. Verify the value on disk rather than assuming a change is needed; if it already reads 110.4, the task is a verification plus a comment/provenance commit, not an edit.

## 4.2 Python

    # USSA-1976 Table 2, Cat. II, as corrected by the errata for NTRS 19770009539:
    # printed 110 K was too small by 0.4 K; correct value 110.4 K.
    SUTHERLAND_S_K: float = 110.4          # K
    SUTHERLAND_BETA: float = 1.458e-6      # kg m^-1 s^-1 K^-0.5

    def viscosity(t_k: float) -> float:
        """Dynamic viscosity, Pa s. t_k in kelvin."""
        if t_k <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError(f"temperature must be positive kelvin, got {t_k!r}")
        return SUTHERLAND_BETA * t_k**1.5 / (t_k + SUTHERLAND_S_K)

## 4.3 C / C++

    /* USSA-1976 Table 2 Cat. II as corrected (errata, NTRS 19770009539):
       printed 110 K was too small by 0.4 K; correct value 110.4 K. */
    #define SUTHERLAND_S_K   110.4
    #define SUTHERLAND_BETA  1.458e-6
    static inline double viscosity_pa_s(double t_k) {
        return SUTHERLAND_BETA * pow(t_k, 1.5) / (t_k + SUTHERLAND_S_K);
    }

## 4.4 Configuration / data file (units explicit)

    {
      "sutherland": {
        "S": 110.4,
        "unit": "K",
        "beta": 1.458e-6,
        "beta_unit": "kg m^-1 s^-1 K^-0.5",
        "source": "U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976, Table 2 Cat. II, as corrected by errata for NTRS 19770009539 (printed 110 K, too small by 0.4 K)"
      }
    }

## 4.5 Load-time guard (catches a stale 110.0 in any representation)

    assert abs(S - 110.4) < 1e-9, f"Sutherland S must be 110.4 K (errata), got {S}"
    assert 100.0 < S < 200.0, "S is in kelvin; 198.72 means it was supplied in degR"

# 5. Units

S is a temperature additive constant, so it must share the temperature unit used for T inside the formula.

| unit of T in code | S to enter |
|---|---|
| K | **110.4** |
| degC difference | **110.4** (a 110.4 K interval equals a 110.4 degC interval) |
| degR (Rankine) | **198.72** (= 110.4 x 1.8) |
| degF difference | **198.72** |

The correction in Rankine is 0.72 degR (0.4 x 1.8), so a Rankine-based code that carries 198.0 must be changed to 198.72. Sutherland's form mu = beta*T^1.5/(T+S) is invariant only when T and S carry the same unit and beta is rescaled consistently; never mix a kelvin S with a Rankine T.

# 6. Numerical impact of the change

Exact ratio (same beta, same T):

    mu(S=110.4) / mu(S=110.0) = (T + 110.0) / (T + 110.4)

Relative change = -0.4 / (T + 110.0), always a decrease, bounded by -0.122% over the tabulated range (worst case at the coldest tabulated temperature).

| T (K) | mu with S=110.0 (Pa s) | mu with S=110.4 (Pa s) | relative change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 216.65 | 1.4234e-5 | 1.4217e-5 | -0.122% |
| 270.00 | 1.7022e-5 | 1.7004e-5 | -0.105% |
| 288.15 | 1.7912e-5 | 1.7894e-5 | -0.100% |
| 1000.00 | 4.1538e-5 | 4.1523e-5 | -0.036% |

(Absolute values computed with beta = 1.458e-6; the relative column is exact from the ratio identity.) Sea-level dynamic viscosity moves from 1.7912e-5 to 1.7894e-5 Pa s, i.e. it lands on the standard published 1.7894e-5. Kinematic viscosity at sea level (rho0 = 1.2250 kg m^-3) moves from 1.4622e-5 to 1.4607e-5 m^2/s. Reynolds number, which scales as 1/mu, rises by 0.100% at 288.15 K and by at most 0.122% anywhere in the tabulated range.

# 7. Verification and regression procedure

1. Unit test on the constant: `S == 110.4` within 1e-12, and the stored unit tag is K (or 198.72 with tag degR).
2. Viscosity golden values (tolerance 1e-9 absolute / 5e-5 relative):
   - T = 288.15 K -> 1.7894e-5 Pa s
   - T = 216.65 K -> 1.4217e-5 Pa s
   - T = 270.00 K -> 1.7004e-5 Pa s
3. Sensitivity test: for T in {216.65, 250, 288.15, 500, 1000} K, assert `mu_new/mu_old == (T+110.0)/(T+110.4)` within 1e-12 against a pre-change baseline build. This is the direct check that only S moved and beta did not.
4. Bound test: assert max relative change over 200 K <= T <= 1000 K is <= 0.13%. A larger diff means something else (e.g. beta, or the 245.4 conductivity coefficient) was also edited.
5. Table/golden-file check: the document's own tabulated viscosities were computed with 110.4, not 110 (S = 110 would give 1.7912e-5 at sea level rather than the published 1.7894e-5). Therefore no standard-atmosphere table regeneration is required and no published table changes; only project-local golden files generated with the buggy 110.0 need regeneration, and their diff must satisfy item 4.
6. Cross-check in CI: grep the tree for `110.0`, `110 `, `198.0` near identifiers matching /suth|SUTH|sutherland/i to catch a second, hard-coded copy of the constant.

# 8. Explicitly out of scope for this change

The same errata list also flags, in the same table: R* on p. 2 differing from p. 3 by a factor of 10^6 (p. 3 is correct, R* = 8314.32 N m kmol^-1 K^-1); r0 too large by a factor of 1000; sigma too large by a factor of 10^9; and the thermal-conductivity column of Table III too small by a factor of 1000. None of these affect S. Raise them as separate tickets so this patch stays reviewable as a one-constant change.

# Validity of PDG Eq. (34.5) at βγ = 0.01

## 1. Answers

**Ask 1 — Does the stated validity region support applying Eq. (34.5) at βγ = 0.01 and claiming the review's few-percent accuracy?** **No.** βγ = 0.01 lies a factor of 10 below the stated lower bound of the region to which the accuracy claim is attached. The review asserts a few-percent accuracy only inside 0.1 ≤ βγ ≤ 1000; outside it the review asserts nothing, so there is no review accuracy to claim at 0.01.

**Ask 2 — βγ region over which that accuracy is stated:** **0.1 ≤ βγ ≤ 1000**, nominal, both limits Z-dependent.

## 2. Source text (verbatim)

2024 Review of Particle Physics, review “Passage of Particles through Matter”, Sec. 34.2.3, sentence immediately following Eq. (34.5):

> “Eq. (34.5) is valid in the region 0.1 . βγ . 1000 with an accuracy of a few percent. At βγ ∼ 0.1 the projectile speed is comparable to atomic electron “speed”, and at βγ ∼ 1000 radiative effects begin to be important (Sec. 34.6). Both limits are Z dependent.”

Source: https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T01:05:18Z, sha256 1b328278e835.

The same sentence, with the same equation number, appears verbatim in the 2022, 2025 and 2026 editions fetched by the harness, so the answer is a stable feature of the review and not an artifact of one revision or one file.

## 3. Why βγ = 0.01 is outside the stated region

1. **It is below the bound, not at it.** 0.01 vs 0.1 is a full decade. This is not a rounding-level excursion that could be argued away.
2. **The review gives the physical reason for the bound, and that reason applies with full force at 0.01.** Its own words: “At βγ ∼ 0.1 the projectile speed is comparable to atomic electron “speed”.” Eq. (34.5) is a Bethe-type form that assumes the projectile is fast compared with the target electrons; below βγ ≈ 0.1 that assumption degrades, and the review says so at the point where it sets the limit. At 0.01 the projectile is ten times slower still.
3. **The claim is a conjunction, not a bare formula.** “Valid in the region 0.1 . βγ . 1000 **with** an accuracy of a few percent.” The accuracy qualifier is scoped to the region. Outside it, the equation is neither endorsed nor given an uncertainty.
4. **The review points elsewhere at this βγ.** “For particles moving more slowly than ≈ 0.01c (more or less the speed of the outer atomic electrons), Lindhard has been quite successful in describing electronic stopping power, which is proportional to β.” βγ = 0.01 corresponds to β = 0.01/√(1+10⁻⁴) = 0.0099995 ≈ 0.01c. The analyst's operating point sits exactly on the boundary the review assigns to the **Lindhard** regime — i.e., the review's own prescription for this speed is a different, non-Bethe description, and one whose accuracy is not stated as a few percent.
5. **The energy-based escape route is also closed.** The review states “Above 0.5–1.0 MeV the correcterd Bethe theory is adequate.” Converting the analyst's point: γ = √(1+βγ²) = 1.00005, so T = Mc²(γ−1) gives **46.9 keV for a proton** and **5.28 keV for a muon**. Both are one to two orders of magnitude below the 0.5–1.0 MeV window, so even the correcterd-Bethe treatment of Sec. 34.2.6 is not licensed at βγ = 0.01 by the review's own criterion. (Self-consistency check: at the lower edge βγ = 0.1 the same conversion gives 4.68 MeV for a proton and 0.527 MeV for a muon — at or above the stated energy window, which is exactly why 0.1 and not 0.01 is the edge.)
6. **Z-dependence does not rescue it.** “Both limits are Z dependent.” The dependence moves the effective edges around, but there is no material for which the review's statement can be read as extending the few-percent claim down to 0.01; the direction of the caveat is to make the edge less sharp, not to move it a decade.
7. **Corroboration from a different edition (labeled as such, not as the 2024 text).** The 2022 review states: “With these corrections, the Bethe treatment is accurate to about 1% down to β ≈ 0.05, or about 1 MeV for protons (0.13 MeV for muons).” β ≈ 0.05 is βγ ≈ 0.05 — still 5× above the analyst's 0.01, and that is the *correcterd* theory, not Eq. (34.5) as printed.

## 4. Numerical demonstration that Eq. (34.5) is out of domain at βγ = 0.01

The cleanest check needs no accuracy claim at all: evaluate the bracket of Eq. (34.5) and see whether the formula returns a physical number. For a z = 1 particle in copper (Z = 29, A = 63.546, I = 322 eV; δ ≈ 0 below the density-effect threshold), with W_max = 2 m_e c² β²γ² for a heavy projectile:

    B = ½ ln( 2 m_e c² β²γ² W_max / I² ) − β² − δ(βγ)/2
    dE/dx = K z² (Z/A) (1/β²) B ,  K = 0.3071 MeV g⁻¹ cm²

| βγ | W_max = 2 m_e c² β²γ² | W_max / I (I = 322 eV) | B | Outcome |
|----|------------------------|--------------------------|---|---------|
| 0.01 | 102.2 eV | 0.317 | **−1.148** | **negative — unphysical** |
| 0.1  | 10.22 keV | 31.7 | +3.45 | positive; at the stated lower edge |
| 3.5  | 12.52 MeV | 3.89×10⁴ | +9.64 | minimum region (sanity anchor) |

At βγ = 0.01 the maximum kinematically allowed energy transfer, W_max = 102 eV, is **below the mean excitation potential of copper, I = 322 eV**, so the log argument drops under unity and the bracket goes negative. Eq. (34.5) as printed then returns a **negative mean mass stopping power** — not a few-percent value, but a result with the wrong sign. This is independent of any accuracy claim and is a two-minute hand check.

Sanity anchor on the same arithmetic: at βγ = 3.5 (near minimum ionizing), the table gives dE/dx = 0.3071 × (29/63.546) × (1/0.9245) × 9.64 = **1.46 MeV g⁻¹ cm²**, against a tabulated copper minimum of ≈1.40 — agreement at the few-percent level, so the arithmetic producing the negative number at 0.01 is validated where the answer is known.

## 5. What the analyst may claim, and what to do instead

| Regime | What may be claimed |
|--------|---------------------|
| 0.1 ≤ βγ ≤ 1000 | Eq. (34.5) with the review's few-percent accuracy, subject to the Z-dependence caveat at both ends and to Sec. 34.2.6 corrections near βγ ≈ 0.1. |
| βγ < 0.1 (including 0.01) | Nothing from this equation's accuracy clause. Use Lindhard-type electronic stopping (∝ β) plus nuclear stopping, or a validated low-energy code (SRIM/ATIMA, PSTAR), or the PDG AtomicNuclearProperties tables/plots, and quote that source's uncertainty — which is not a few percent at 0.01. |
| Any βγ, thin detector | The few-percent statement is about the **mean** mass stopping power of a moderately relativistic heavy particle, not about a measured energy loss. The review is explicit: “Even with samples of hundreds of events a dependable value for the mean energy loss cannot be obtained.” Use the most-probable energy loss (Sec. 34.2.9) or a restricted energy loss (mean of the 50%–70% smallest samples); no few-percent claim transfers to those estimators. |
| Heavy projectiles (ions) | Additional terms are required; the review notes changes “by a factor of two or more for the heaviest nuclei in certain kinematic regimes.” |

**Recommended wording for the analysis note** (replaces any sentence of the form “we use PDG Eq. (34.5), accurate to a few percent”):

> The stopping power at βγ = 0.01 is taken from [low-energy code / table], not from PDG Eq. (34.5). Eq. (34.5) is stated in the 2024 Review of Particle Physics to be valid over 0.1 ≤ βγ ≤ 1000 with a few-percent accuracy (Z-dependent limits); βγ = 0.01 lies a decade below that region, and evaluation of the printed equation there returns a non-physical (negative) mean stopping power for a z = 1 projectile in copper. The few-percent accuracy of Eq. (34.5) is therefore not claimed for this operating point.

## 6. How this memo handles the harness's proof of absence (auditability note)

Ask 2 is **not** listed as not-stated, and nothing is blocked. The page states the region verbatim (Sec. 2 above), so there is an answer to give. The harness's proof of absence covers a different proposition: it shows that no statement of a **0.01–0.1** window (“0.01 ≤ βγ ≤ 0.1”, “βγ between 0.01 and 0.1”, “βγ in the range 0.01–0.1”, “valid for βγ ≈ 0.01–0.1”, “applicable βγ region: 0.01–0.1”, “relativistic boost factor βγ = 0.01–0.1”) appears anywhere in the full text of the 2024 review (39 pages, 87,263 characters) or of the 2024 Booklet (288 pages, 565,991 characters). That is exactly the proposition the analyst's use requires, and its absence is positive evidence for the **No** in ask 1: there is no reading of the page under which a few-percent claim at βγ = 0.01 is inside the stated region. It is not evidence that the page states no region at all, since it states 0.1–1000 in as many words.

## 7. One-line summary for the record

Eq. (34.5) is stated valid for 0.1 ≤ βγ ≤ 1000 at a few-percent accuracy (Z-dependent limits); βγ = 0.01 is outside that region by a decade, and the review's own low-βγ and low-energy guidance routes such a case to Lindhard/ correcterd-Bethe treatments instead. The use is not supported.

The first reads: "35.6.5), the same end is often accomplished by using a restricted energy loss, the mean of 50%–70% of the samples with the smallest signals as the estimator."

TECHNICAL NOTE — THE SUM OF NEUTRINO MASSES Σmν IN PLANCK 2018 RESULTS VI (arXiv:1807.06209v4)

0. BOTTOM LINE
Planck 2018 does not measure Σmν. Version v4 of arXiv:1807.06209, combining Planck with BAO, quotes a 95% confidence UPPER LIMIT of 0.12 eV — not a measured value, not a detection, and not a central value with an uncertainty. A report that needs "a measured neutrino-mass sum from Planck 2018" therefore has no measurement to quote from this source; it must either present the number explicitly as an upper limit or state that no measurement exists.

1. ASK 2 — VERDICT: NO.
The result combining Planck 2018 with BAO does not quote a measured value for Σmν. In v4 the Σmν entries are written as one-sided inequalities, with no central value, no ± uncertainty, and no statement of a detection:
  • "∑mν<0.12 eV (95%, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO)."
  • "∑mν<0.60 eV (95%, Planck lensing+BAO+θMC)."
Both are bounds of the form Σmν < x at 95% confidence. Cosmological data of this type place an upper bound on the sum of neutrino masses (a non-detection consistent with the minimum mass implied by neutrino oscillations); nothing in the source supports writing either number as "Σmν = 0.12 eV".

2. ASK 3 — EXACT CONSTRAINT AND THE CONFIDENCE LEVEL FOR UPPER LIMITS.
Constraint, quoted verbatim in form from v4, for the Planck+BAO combination:
  Σmν < 0.12 eV (95%, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO)
The second Σmν entry in the same list, which is a different (weaker) combination and must not be substituted for the BAO one:
  Σmν < 0.60 eV (95%, Planck lensing+BAO+θMC)
Confidence level the abstract assigns to upper limits: 95% (i.e. a 95% one-sided upper confidence limit, ≈2σ). Every Σmν statement in v4, in the abstract and in the results, is quoted at 95% confidence; there is no 68% CL central value for Σmν to report, because no such value is given.

3. ASK 1 — NO MEASURED VALUE IS STATED (report-ready wording).
There is no measured neutrino-mass sum in Planck 2018 to supply to the report. Correct and incorrect phrasings for the report text:
  ✔ CORRECT: "Planck 2018 (TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO) constrains the sum of neutrino masses to Σmν < 0.12 eV (95% CL). This is an upper limit, not a measurement."
  ✘ WRONG: "Planck 2018 measures Σmν = 0.12 eV." (Converts a bound into a point estimate.)
  ✘ WRONG: "Planck 2018 measures Σmν = 0.12 ± 0.04 eV." (No uncertainty on Σmν is quoted in the source; the ± would be invented.)
  ✘ WRONG: quoting Σmν = 0.27 ± 0.08 eV as a Planck 2018 result. That figure is from Hoeneisen (arXiv:1811.07894), a third-party combination of SDSS BAO with Planck and direct σ8 measurements; it is not a Planck Collaboration result and must not be attributed to arXiv:1807.06209.

If the report's template strictly requires a value with a central estimate and an error bar, the Planck 2018 row must be marked "upper limit only — no measurement", and a measured Σmν must be sourced elsewhere (e.g. laboratory β-decay or cosmological + external-data combinations), not from this paper.

4. WORDING RULES FOR DOWNSTREAM USE
  • Always carry the data combination with the number; the two Σmν numbers in v4 are not interchangeable.
  • Always carry the confidence level (95%) and the inequality sign (<).
  • Never describe the bound as a detection, a measurement, a best fit, or a constraint at 68% CL.
  • Unit is eV for Σmν throughout.

5. PROVENANCE AND SCOPE OF THIS NOTE
All quotations are from the HTML rendering of version v4, https://arxiv.org/html/1807.06209v4 (532,096 characters, fetched 2026-11-23T01:08:24Z, sha256 314c6ee4a8fc). ## 0. Bottom line

| Item | Answer |
|---|---|
| Value of Rj | **71,398** |
| Unit | **km** (kilometres); equivalently 7.1398 x 10^4 km = 7.1398 x 10^7 m |
