The public planetary reference that carries an explicit definition of the symbol Rj is the NSSDC Jupiter Fact Sheet, in the "Jovian Magnetosphere" block. Quoted verbatim from the retrieved page:

> Jovian Magnetosphere
> Model GSFC-O6
> Dipole field strength: 4.30 Gauss-Rj3
> Dipole tilt to rotational axis: 9.4 degrees
> Longitude of tilt: 200.1 degrees
> Dipole offset: 0.119 Rj
> Surface (1 Rj) field strength: 4.0 - 13.0 Gauss
> **Rj denotes Jovian model radius, defined here to be 71,398 km**

The same panel is headed by a reference epoch line: "Reference Date : 12:00 UT 1 Jan 2000 (JD 2451545.0)". (The "Gauss-Rj3" in the plain-text extraction is "Gauss-Rj^3" on the rendered page; the exponent is lost in text extraction, not in the source.)

## 2. Ask 1 — numerical value and unit

- **71,398 km.**
- Conversions for the worksheet: 71,398 km = 7.1398 x 10^4 km = 7.1398 x 10^7 m = 71,398,000 m. (In statute miles, 71,398 / 1.609344 = 44,365 mi, to 5 s.f.)
- **Precision handling:** the reference prints five significant figures with no decimal and no uncertainty, and introduces the number with "defined here to be", i.e. it is a *defined constant*, not a measurement with an error bar. Carry 71,398 km as exact in the worksheet. If any downstream product rounds it, it must say so — do not silently render it as 71,400 km or 7.14 x 10^4 km.

**Note on the proof of absence.** The harness's absence proof for ask 1 covers strings that would assert **71,492 km** (e.g. "R_J = 71,492 km", "Jovian model radius = 71,492 km", "R_J = 7.1492x10^7 m") on the NSSDC fact sheet, the LASP/JPL Jupiter appendix, and Wikipedia's *Jupiter radius* article. Those strings are indeed absent — which is consistent with, and corroborates, the fact that the fact sheet's model-radius line gives **71,398 km**, not 71,492 km. The page therefore does **not** state "none": it states a figure, in words, and that figure is 71,398 km. Ask 1 is accordingly answered here and is deliberately not listed in `not_stated`.

## 3. Ask 2 — how the reference defines Rj

The definition has four components, all readable from the quoted panel:

1. **By stipulation, not measurement.** The operative words are "defined here to be". Rj is a *convention* fixed at 71,398 km so that model quantities have a stable normalisation; it is not derived from, and does not track, improved geodesy.
2. **Named quantity: "Jovian model radius".** That is the reference's own term of art. It is a model length, in the sense of "the length unit in which this magnetospheric model is expressed".
3. **Scope: the Jovian magnetosphere model GSFC-O6** (the O6 tilted-dipole model, Connerney 1993 family), on the same panel, at reference epoch J2000 (JD 2451545.0). Rj is the normalising length for that model's field quantities, as its own usage shows:
   - dipole field strength in **Gauss-Rj^3** (a moment normalised by Rj cubed);
   - dipole **offset 0.119 Rj** (a length in units of Rj);
   - **surface (1 Rj) field strength 4.0 - 13.0 Gauss** (the 1-Rj shell is the model's surface).
4. **Negative content, which is the point of the line.** It is *not* the volumetric mean radius, *not* the 1-bar equatorial radius, and *not* the polar radius — even though the very same fact sheet publishes all three a few lines earlier under "Bulk parameters": Equatorial radius (1 bar level) 71,492 km; Polar radius 66,854 km; Volumetric mean radius 69,911 km. The definition sentence exists precisely to stop a reader from substituting any of those measured radii into a magnetospheric calculation.

## 4. Why 71,398 km and not 71,492 km — provenance

The number is not a stray. It is the radius convention that travels with the O6/Connerney magnetic model. Corroboration from the LASP/JPL *Jupiter* appendix (https://lasp.colorado.edu/mop/files/2015/08/jupiter_appendix2-1.pdf, sha256 84d4f6f6f7c4):

and, in the note to Table A2.5:

> (Campbell and Synnott (1985) use a radius of 71398 km, so there is a slight difference in these moments.)

Same moment (4.300 gauss), same tilt (9.4 deg), same tilt longitude (200.1 deg), same offset (0.119 Rj) — i.e. the same model — and the radius attached to it is 71,398 km. The value is within 94 km (0.13 %) of the 1-bar equatorial radius 71,492 km and within 2 km of the ionospheric radius 71,400 km (Dessler 1983, LASP Table A2.4), which is exactly why an explicit definition line was needed.

## 5. Disambiguation table — the radii a worksheet must not confuse

| Radius | Value | Where it comes from | Is it Rj? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Jovian model radius, Rj** | **71,398 km** | NSSDC Jupiter Fact Sheet, Jovian Magnetosphere panel (GSFC-O6) | **Yes — this is the answer** |
| Equatorial radius (1 bar level) | 71,492 km | NSSDC fact sheet, Bulk parameters | No — measured 1-bar equatorial |

The last row is the most common trap: Wikipedia's *Jupiter radius* article defines the **unit** RJ = 71,492 km (IAU nominal equatorial, exact 7.1492 x 10^7 m, with nominal polar 6.6854 x 10^7 m). That is a unit-of-length convention for describing object sizes; it is not the magnetospheric model radius Rj. A worksheet that says "Rj = Jovian model radius" is using the NSSDC/GSFC-O6 convention, and 71,398 km is the matching number.

## Bottom line

**Ask 1 (the illustration).** The 2024 PDG review *Passage of Particles Through Matter* does not use a figure for this; it uses a one-sentence worked example placed immediately after Eq. (34.9), as the closing paragraph of Sec. 34.2.7 and immediately before Sec. 34.2.8 ("Restricted energy loss rates for relativistic ionizing particles"). Verbatim:

> "δ rays of even modest energy are rare. For a β ≈ 1 particle, for example, on average only one collision with Te > 10 keV will occur along a path length of 90 cm of argon gas [1]."

Its companion illustration, two paragraphs earlier in the same section, is: "Most frequently the energy losses are small (for 90% of all collisions the energy losses are less than 100 eV)." Together these two sentences are the review's illustration of how steep the knock-on (δ-ray) spectrum of Eq. (34.9) is: the overwhelming majority of collisions are sub-100 eV, and hard knock-ons are rare.

**Ask 2 (the number).** For a β ≈ 1 particle, the average number of collisions with Te > 10 keV along 90 cm of argon gas is **1** (one collision, on average).

**Citation for traceability:** PDG 2024, *Passage of Particles Through Matter* (Sec. 34.2, Rev. 34.2.7, paragraph following Eq. 34.9), PDF stamp "25th March, 2025", https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf. The identical sentence (same wording, same "one … 90 cm … argon") appears in the 2019 (Eq. 33.9), 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025-reprint and 2026 editions of the review, so the citation is stable across editions — only the equation/section numbers shift.

## 1. What exactly the review says, and what it does not say

- **Quantity defined:** the *mean number of δ-ray producing collisions per track*, i.e. inelastic collisions in which the energy transfer W to a knock-on electron exceeds Te = 10 keV (kinetic energy of the secondary). It is not a dose, not an energy deposit, and not a per-unit-length rate — it is a count per 90 cm of path.
- **Primary:** a heavy (m z, z = 1) particle with β ≈ 1. The sentence sits in Sec. 34.2, "Electronic energy loss by heavy particles". For an *electron* primary the knock-on process is Møller scattering and this number does not apply; recompute from the Møller cross section rather than quoting it.
- **Gas state:** the sentence gives no pressure or temperature. As shown below, the printed "one" is reproduced by argon at NTP (≈1.66–1.78 g/L). If your detector gas is at a different density, scale linearly (Sec. 3).
- **Reference marker:** "[1]" in the sentence is the review's own citation marker, not a page or equation number.

## 2. Reproduction check (why "one" is the right number)

Integrating the review's own Eq. (34.9), d²N/(dT dx) = ½ K z² (Z/A) (1/β²) F(T)/T², from Te = 10 keV to Wmax, with F(T) ≈ 1 (the spin-½ correction 1 − β²Te/Wmax is ≈ 10⁻³ here, and Eq. (34.9)'s known inaccuracy near T ≈ I is irrelevant at 10 keV):

    N(>Te) = ½ · K · z² · (Z/A) · (1/β²) · [ 1/Te − 1/Wmax ] · (ρ·L)

with K = 0.307075 MeV mol⁻¹ g⁻¹ cm², z = 1, β = 1, Z/A(Ar) = 18/39.948 = 0.4506, Te = 0.010 MeV, ρ·L in g/cm².

The 1/Wmax term is negligible (10 keV/12.5 MeV ≈ 8×10⁻⁴ at βγ ≈ 3.5, smaller still at higher γ), so:

    ½ K (Z/A) / Te = 0.15354 × 0.4506 / 0.01 = 6.92 per g/cm²

For 90 cm of argon (molar volume 22.414 L/mol at 0 °C, 1 atm):

| Gas temperature | ρ (g/L) | ρ·L over 90 cm (g/cm²) | N(>10 keV) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 °C | 1.782 | 0.1604 | 1.11 |
| 20 °C | 1.661 | 0.1495 | 1.03 |
| 25 °C | 1.633 | 0.1470 | 1.02 |

So the printed "only one collision … along 90 cm of argon gas" is argon at NTP, and my independent recomputation lands at 1.02–1.11 — i.e. "one" to the precision the review quotes. There is no tension between the quoted figure and the underlying cross section.

## 3. Scaling rules for the detector-background budget

Use these to move the review's illustration to your actual gas, pressure and path length. They follow directly from the same integral and are consistent with the numbers above.

    N(>Te) = 6.92 × (10 keV / Te) × (1/β²) × (Z/A)/0.4506 × ρ[g/cm³] × L[cm]

- **Path length:** linear. 1 m of argon at NTP ≈ 1.1–1.2 δ rays > 10 keV; 9 cm ≈ 0.1.
- **Pressure/density:** linear in ρ. A 1 bar, 20 °C fill is the reference; a 10 bar argon fill multiplies the count by ≈10 (≈11 per 90 cm). Always record the gas density alongside any quoted δ-ray rate — this is the single largest source of order-of-magnitude error in a background budget.
- **Threshold:** N ∝ 1/Te above threshold. Dropping to 5 keV doubles the count; raising to 20 keV halves it.
- **Gas species:** N ∝ ⟨Z/A⟩ (approximately), and per unit length ∝ ρ⟨Z/A⟩. For P10 (90% Ar / 10% CH4) ⟨Z/A⟩ ≈ 0.456, i.e. within 1% of pure argon — the review's number carries over unchanged at the same density.
- **β:** N ∝ 1/β². At β = 1 the correction is unity; at β = 0.9 it is 1.23.

## 4. Statistics and energy for the budget

- The collisions are independent and rare, so the count per track is Poisson with mean μ = 1 (reference case): P(0) = 36.8%, P(1) = 36.8%, P(≥1) = 63.2%, P(≥2) = 26.4%. A single 90 cm argon track therefore has a ~1-in-4 chance of producing two or more >10 keV δ rays; budget the tail, not just the mean.
- Mean energy carried by those δ rays (derived here, **not** printed in the review): ½ K (Z/A) ln(Wmax/Te) × ρL ≈ 0.0692 × 7.1 × 0.15 ≈ 0.074 MeV, i.e. ≈70 keV per 90 cm of NTP argon at βγ ≈ 3.5, growing only logarithmically with γ. With a mean count of 1, the typical >10 keV δ ray carries ~70 keV — that is the number to propagate into the energy-deposit/background estimate, not the 10 keV threshold.

Quote it as: "PDG 2024, Passage of Particles Through Matter, Sec. 34.2 (paragraph following Eq. 34.9): a β ≈ 1 particle makes on average one collision with Te > 10 keV per 90 cm of argon gas (NTP)." Then attach your own scaled figure computed from Sec. 3 with your detector's actual fill density and track length, and state the density explicitly.
